ASE calculates the static and dynamic effects of general loading on any type of structure. To start the calculations the user divides the structure to be analyzed into an assembly of individual elements interconnected at nodes (Finite Element Method). Possible types of elements are : haunched beams, springs, cables, truss elements, plane triangular or quadrilateral shell elements and three-dimensional continuum elements.
 The program handles structures with rigid or elastic types of support. An elastic support can be applied to an area, a line or at nodal points. Rigid elements or skew supports can be taken into account.
 ASE calculates the effects of nodal, line and block loads. The loads can be defined indepen- dently from the selected element mesh. The generation of loads from stresses of a primary load case allows the consideration of construction stages, redistribution and creep effects.
 Non-linear calculations enables the user to take the failure of particular elements into account, such as: cables in compression, uplifting of supported plates, yielding, friction or crack effects for spring and foundation elements. Non-linear materials are available for three-dimensional and shell elements. Geometrical non-linear computations allow the investigation of 2nd and 3rd order theory effects by cable, beam, shell and volume structures.
 In case of beam structures, the program can calculate warping torsion with up to 7 degrees of freedom per node.
 The user of ASE should therefore gather experience from simple examples before tackling more complicated structures. A check of the results through approximate engineering calcula- tions is imperative.
 The basic version of ASE performs the linear analyses of beams, cables, trusses, plane and volume structures. Plain strain and rotational systems can be analyzed with TALPA.
 Extended versions of ASE offer calculations of:
 • Influence surfaces
 • Non-linear analyses
 • Pile elements with linear/parabolic soil coefficient distribution
 • Creep and shrinkage
 • Forces from construction stages
 • Modal analysis, Time step method
 • Material non-linearities
 • Geometrical non-linearities
 • Membrane elements

A continuum or a plane structure can be interpreted as a statically or geometrically infinitely indeterminate structure. If an analytical solution is unknown, every numerically approximate method is based on converting this infinite system into a finite one, in other words to discretizing it.
 The advantage of the finite elements lies in their universal applicability to any geometrical shape and almost to any loading. This is achieved by a modular principle. Single elements which describe parts of the structure in a computer oriented manner are assembled into a complete structure.
 The continuous structure is represented thus by a large but finite number of elements. A discrete solution consisting of n unknowns is calculated instead of the continuous solution. In general, the approximate solution may represent the exact solution better with the use of more elements. The single elements of an area can be of arbitrarily small dimensions in comparison to the dimensions of the overall structure without giving rise to any incompatibilities with the presented theory. The refinement of the subdivision is, however, subjected to certain limitations due to numerical reasons.
 The Finite Element Method (FEM) employed in ASE is a displacement method, meaning that the unknowns are deformation values at several selected points, the so-called nodes. Displace- ments can be obtained with an element-wise interpolation of the nodal values. The calculation of the mechanical behaviour is based generally on an energy principle (minimisation of the deformation work). The result is a so-called stiffness matrix. This matrix specifies the reaction forces at the nodes of an element when these nodes are subjected to known displacements.
 The global force equilibrium is generated then for each node in order to determine the un- knowns. A force in the same direction which is a function of this or another displacement corresponds to each displacement. This leads to a system of equations with n unknowns, where n can become very large. Numerically beneficial banded matrices result, however, due to the local character of the element-wise interpolation.

 The second step is that with most CPU time. It may use up to 90 percent of the total CPU time. However, it has to occur only once for a static system.
 The stresses jumps from element to element. The size of the jump is thus a direct measure of the quality of the FE analysis.

The table at hand summarizes which finite‐element types in the ASE program can participate in non‐linear analyses—both material and geometrical—and flags license restrictions that may preclude their use under certain ASE modules (SEPP or PFAHL).  Below is a structured walkthrough of every column, each element row, and the accompanying footnotes:

1. Columns  
   • “Element”: the short name of the finite‐element type in ASE.  
   • “Non‐linear Material”: indicates whether the element’s constitutive behavior can go beyond linear elasticity.  Where applicable, it lists special failure or nonlinear phenomena (tension failure, compression failure, elastic‐bedding only, etc.).  
   • “Geometrical Non‐linearity”: indicates whether large‐displacement/large‐rotation effects are accounted for in the element formulation (e.g., cable sag, overall stiffness change when deformed).  

2. Rows (Element by Element)  
   1. SPRI (spring element)  
      – Material: yes (fully nonlinear constitutive law possible)  
      – Geometry: yes (accounts for geometric stiffening/softening)  
      – License: no footnote → available with any ASE license (ASE core, SEPP, or PFAHL)  
   2. TRUS (truss element)  
      – Material: yes, with explicit tension‐failure capability (material springs lose load‐carrying capacity in tension when a threshold is exceeded)  
      – Geometry: yes (large‐displacement formulation included)  
      – License: no footnote → available with all licenses  
   3. CABL (cable element)  
      – Material: yes, plus a compression‐failure model (cables can’t carry compression and will buckle/fail)  
      – Geometry: yes, including cable‐sag effects under self‐weight or applied loads  
      – License: no footnote → available with all licenses  
   4. BEAM (beam or frame element)  
      – Material: yes (nonlinear bending, axial effects possible)  
      – Geometry: yes (P–Δ and large‐rotation effects included)  
      – License: no footnote → available with all licenses  
   5. PILE¹ (pile/shaft element)  
      – Material: elastic bedding only (the soil–structure interaction is limited to linear‐elastic springs along the element)  
      – Geometry: yes (accounts for large displacements/rotations of the pile)  
      – License restriction (footnote ¹): not available under the SEPP license  
   6. QUAD² (quadrilateral shell/solid element)  
      – Material: yes (full material nonlinearity in-plane or through-thickness)  
      – Geometry: yes (large‐strain/large‐rotation capability)  
      – License restriction (footnote ²): not available under the PFAHL license  
   7. BRIC¹² (brick or hexahedral solid element)  
      – Material: yes (supports material‐nonlinear constitutive models in 3D)  
      – Geometry: yes (geometric stiffness included)  
      – License restrictions:  
         • ¹ Not available with SEPP  
         • ² Not available with PFAHL  
   8. BOUN (boundary or connector element)  
      – Material: – (no nonlinear material modeling implemented)  
      – Geometry: – (no geometric‐nonlinearity support)  
      – License: available under any license, but only for linear analysis  
   9. FLEX¹² (flexible link or specialized connector)  
      – Material: – (linear only)  
      – Geometry: – (no large‐displacement)  
      – License restrictions:  
         • ¹ SEPP does not include FLEX  
         • ² PFAHL does not include FLEX  
  10. Halfspace² (infinite‐domain foundation or soil half‐space)  
      – Material: yes (nonlinear soil models can be assigned)  
      – Geometry: – (geometric nonlinearity of the half‐space itself is not modeled)  
      – License: not available under PFAHL (footnote ²)

3. Footnotes & Licensing  
   – Footnote ¹: Elements marked “¹” (PILE, BRIC, FLEX) cannot be used if you only have the SEPP license installed.  
   – Footnote ²: Elements marked “²” (QUAD, BRIC, FLEX, Halfspace) cannot be used under the PFAHL license.  
   – Non‐linear analyses (either material or geometrical) additionally require a higher‐level ASE license, above the basic core.  

4. Contextual Notes  
   – ASE, SEPP, and PFAHL are three licensing tiers/modules of the same program suite.  Depending on which modules are activated, some elements are entirely unavailable, even in linear mode.  
   – Section 3.41 of the ASE documentation contains a comprehensive list of all nonlinear formulations and failure criteria supported.  
   – Users planning large‐displacement or advanced material failure analyses should verify both element capabilities and license entitlements before setting up their models.

The figure, titled “Figure 2.1: Column geometric nonlinear theory 2nd and 3rd order,” is composed of two adjacent schematic diagrams, each illustrating the deformed shape of a slender vertical column under combined loading, contrasted for second-order (TH2) and third-order (TH3) geometric nonlinear analyses.

Left diagram (TH2):
- The base of the column is rigidly supported (depicted by a hatched block at the bottom). The column’s original, undeformed axis is a straight vertical line rising from the base.
- A horizontal force Px is applied at the top node, shown by a left-to-right arrow labeled “Px.”
- Simultaneously, a vertical compressive force Pz is applied downward at the same top node, indicated by a downward arrow labeled “Pz.”
- Under TH2 theory (often called the P-Δ or pi-delta method), the axial compression Pz reduces the effective stiffness of the column but equilibrium is still enforced on the undeformed (original) geometry. As a result the column deflects laterally in X, following a single curving line (drawn with a relatively thin stroke).
- A vector at the deformed tip, labeled “dux – TH2,” marks the lateral displacement produced purely by the second-order effect.
- No out-of-plane (Z-direction) deflection occurs here (indicated parenthetically in the surrounding text as “no duz!”).

Right diagram (TH3):
- Again, the column stands on a rigid base and carries the same vertical load, Pz.
- Under full geometric nonlinear analysis (TH3), the equilibrium equations are solved iteratively on the continuously updated, deformed configuration rather than the original straight shape.
- The column therefore follows a slightly different, more physically accurate curved profile (plotted as a thicker, more pronounced bending line), reflecting the additional effect of axial force acting along the deflected geometry.
- At the top, the total lateral displacement vector is labeled “u – TH3,” denoting the combined first-, second-, and higher-order geometric contributions.  
- Because the actual bent shape is used for computing internal forces, the third-order result shows a subtly stiffer response (less total deflection) than a naïve second-order estimate—this is seen by comparing the two curve radii.

Key distinctions highlighted by this comparison:
• TH2 treats geometric stiffness in a linearized sense about the original shape, producing an additional lateral deflection dux but ignoring updates to the structure’s tangent stiffness path.  
• TH3 enforces equilibrium on the real, continuously updating geometry, leading to an internally consistent bending plus axial‐extension interaction.  
• Only in TH3 (for beam, quad and brick finite elements) are rigid‐body motions explicitly subtracted so that computed stresses stem solely from pure deformational strains.

The provided illustration (labelled “Figure 2.2”) consists of two side-by-side, schematic line‐drawings of an identical simply supported girder, each subjected to the same uniformly distributed vertical load. The purpose is to contrast the behavior predicted by SOFiSTiK’s second‐order (TH2) geometric theory with that predicted by its full geometric nonlinear, third‐order (TH3) theory. Both sketches share these common features:  
• A straight, horizontal beam drawn as a single curved line once it deflects under load.  
• Two support symbols at the ends: triangular supports indicating that vertical movement is restrained, and small horizontal bars indicating that horizontal movement (in the x‐direction) is held fixed.  
• A series of equally spaced downward‐pointing arrows along the top of the span, representing a continuous vertical load.  

Left‐hand sketch:  
• Captioned beneath as “TH2 : N = 0.”  
• Under the uniform vertical load, the beam deflects into a symmetric “smile”‐shape: its midspan displacement is purely vertical, and the deformed curve bows downward.  
• There is no axial or normal force in the beam—TH2 neglects any axial stiffening or softening induced by the deflection geometry. Consequently, the beam simply bends under the load without any change in its overall length.  

Right‐hand sketch:  
• Captioned “TH3 : N.”  
• Under the same loading and support conditions, the deflected shape is noticeably flatter; the mid‐span displacement is reduced compared to the TH2 case.  
• Because both ends are fixed in the horizontal (x) direction, any vertical deflection entails a geometric increase in the beam’s arc length. In the TH3 (third‐order) analysis, that induced axial strain generates a tensile normal force “N,” which carries a portion of the applied vertical load.  
• The combination of bending and axial action results in a stiffer response (smaller deflection) than the pure‐bending, zero‐axial‐force result of the TH2 model.  

Overall caption (below the two sketches):  
“Figure 2.2: girder left+right fixed in x ! : TH3 induces a load carrying normal force N”  

Key points illustrated by the pair of diagrams:  
- In TH2 (second‐order “pi‐delta” theory), geometric nonlinearity is only partially accounted for through an equivalent stiffness reduction from pre‐existing axial loads; here, with no axial load initially, the beam simply deflects under bending.  
- In TH3 (full geometric nonlinear analysis), equilibrium is enforced on the actual deformed configuration. The supports’ x‐fixity transforms vertical deflection into axial extension, producing a normal force that stiffens the element and reduces its vertical deflection.  
This visual succinctly highlights why TH3 yields a more physically accurate prediction for beam‐type elements when significant deflections produce non‐negligible axial effects.

The image is a schematic line drawing intended to illustrate how, under a fully geometric nonlinear (third­-order, TH3) analysis in SOFiSTiK, the total displacement field of a beam element can be decomposed into a rigid‐body motion plus a pure deformation that induces stresses. It uses three overlaid curve segments and two distinct arrow styles to make the point:

1. Base Configuration (leftmost blue line)  
   - Drawn as a straight slender line in solid blue, labeled “Base configuration.”  
   - This represents the original, undeformed shape of the structural member before any loads or displacements take effect.  

2. Rigid‐Body Motion (curved black arrow)  
   - A single thick black arrow, drawn between the Base configuration and the next curve, is labeled “Rigid body motion.”  
   - Its curved trajectory indicates a rotation (and possible translation) that carries the entire element from its initial position into a new orientation, without altering its shape.  

3. Co-Rotated Configuration (middle blue curve)  
   - Rendered in a lighter blue than the Base configuration, this slightly curved line shows the member after the rigid‐body rotation/translation but prior to any internal deformation.  
   - It retains the length and cross-section properties of the original, capturing only gross motion and alignment with the load path.  

4. Pure Deformation (curly red arrow)  
   - A slender, curved arrow swooping from the co-rotated curve to the final configuration, labeled “Pure deformation.”  
   - The arrow’s spiral or curly shape visually distinguishes it from the rigid‐body arrow, emphasizing that this step involves shape change (bending, stretching) rather than just motion.  

5. Current Configuration (rightmost red curve)  
   - Shown in bold red, this final curve is more pronouncedly bent and displaced, representing the actual deformed geometry under load.  
   - Labeled “Current configuration,” it embodies both the rigid‐body repositioning and the elastic/plastic deformations of the member.  

Through these layered graphics, the figure communicates the key principle of TH3: the total displacement vector at each point is split into a part that stems from gross element motion (which does not generate stresses) and a part that is the “pure” deformation responsible for internal force resultants. By subtracting out the rigid‐body component, the analysis isolates bending, shear and axial strains in the co-rotated frame, thereby ensuring that only deformation-induced strains feed into the constitutive laws. This decomposition is unique to the full geometric nonlinearity of TH3 and does not occur in the simpler second‐order (TH2) Pi-delta approach.

 In the column example in figure 2.1 the effect of theory TH2 causes a stiffness reduction in the column due to the compression normal force (geometric stiffness). The bottom bending moment increases due to the displacement of the vertical load Pz. This type of analysis is also known as pi-delta method.
 In the complete geometric nonlinear analysis TH3 the column head follows the physically cor- rect path. Equilibrium is iterated on the real deformed shape.

 deflects vertical without a normal force N:
 In the TH3 analysis the vertical displacement causes a lengthing of the beam. The created normal force N carries a part of the load and reduces the vertical deformation.

The provided image is a two-panel schematic comparing how internal forces in a slender, cantilevered beam element are defined under second-order (“TH2”) and third-order (“TH3”) geometric nonlinear theories. A line of caption text below both panels reads: “Definition of forces in geometric nonlinear theory 2nd and 3rd order.”

Left Panel (TH2):
- A vertical support symbol at the bottom indicates a fixed root. From that support, the beam initially follows a very slight curvature toward the right.
- At the beam’s free end (top), two orthogonal arrows originate:
  • The arrow labeled “N” points strictly upward, aligned with the original, undeformed global vertical axis.  
  • The arrow labeled “VZ” points horizontally to the right, coinciding with the original global transverse (Z-direction) axis.
- These arrows illustrate that, in the second-order (TH2) formulation, internal forces are always resolved in the undeformed, original coordinate system. Accordingly, the axial force N remains vertical regardless of the beam’s deformed shape, and the shear force VZ remains horizontal.
- Below the beam, the label “TH2” identifies this panel as the second-order theory.

Right Panel (TH3):
- Again, a fixed support is shown at the bottom, and the beam has an identical slight rightward curvature. However, the key difference is that the local force axes have rotated to follow the deformed geometry.
- At the free end, two arrows labeled “N” and “VZ” are attached tangentially to the curved beam:
  • The “N” arrow is now inclined, pointing along the beam’s tangent at its tip, indicating that the normal (axial) force is taken in the deformed coordinate direction.  
  • The “VZ” arrow is also rotated, pointing roughly outward and slightly downward, showing that the shear force is resolved in the local deformed Z-direction of the element.
- This illustrates the third-order (TH3) approach, where internal forces (axial N, bending moments MY/MZ, and torsional moment MT) are always referred to the beam’s own, current (deformed) cross-section axes.  
- Below this beam, the label “TH3” identifies the third-order theory.

Additional Context (from accompanying text):
- In TH2, shear forces are strictly transversal in the original frame; a vertical column’s N stays vertical and VZ stays horizontal irrespective of actual deflection.
- In TH3, the forces N, MY and MZ relate to the center of gravity of each active partial section (rather than to the node-connecting line), while MT, VY and VZ are related to the center of shear.
- Since version 2016, dead loads are applied at the center of mass, meaning any eccentricity between the center of mass and center of stiffness is automatically accounted for in the nonlinear analysis.

Together, these two diagrams concisely contrast how second-order and third-order geometric nonlinear beam theories handle the orientation of internal forces relative to either the original or the continuously deformed element axes.

The image is a two‐part schematic entitled “Figure 2.6: T‐Beam Philosophy.” Each part shows a thin horizontal grid of quadrilateral finite‐element plate (slab) elements represented by straight lines and small circles at each corner node, intersected by a T‐shaped beam cross section oriented vertically. The purpose of the illustration is to show how a centric beam and slab overlap in a standard finite‐element model and how the “T‐beam philosophy” corrects for double definition of concrete in the overlap.

1. Upper Diagram (Standard Overlap)  
   - A regular mesh of plate elements spans from left to right. Nodes are drawn as small open circles at every corner of each quad, forming a rectangular grid.  
   - In the middle of the mesh, a T‐beam profile is inserted: its flange (the horizontal top of the “T”) sits flush with the mesh plane, while its stem (the vertical web) extends downward below the mesh. The beam cross section is shown in medium gray, with its flange overlapping part of the slab mesh above.  
   - Some of the plate element lines pass directly through the beam flange, indicating that both slab and beam occupy the same region of concrete. This overlap leads to double counting of stiffness and dead load if not corrected.

2. Lower Diagram (Visualization Adjustment)  
   - The same slab mesh appears, but here the beam cross section is shown displaced slightly downward so that the top of the T‐beam flange lies just beneath the slab’s bottom surface. In this view, the mesh and beam do not visually penetrate one another.  
   - The beam nodes along its flange edge now align in a straight line just below the plate nodes, emphasizing the offset. Small circles mark the beam’s nodes; the slab nodes remain in their original grid above.  
   - A single plate element row directly above the beam flange is highlighted, illustrating where nodes would be coupled via kinematic constraints.

Key features conveyed by the figure:  
- The “centric” positioning of the beam in the node plane is such that its centroid lies slightly below the slab mid‐thickness, causing partial protrusion of the flange through the slab in the raw model.  
- To simplify visualization (e.g. in WinGRAF or ANIMATOR), the entire beam is shifted downward so that its upper surface lines up with the bottom of the slab. This avoids the appearance of intersection in rendered views.  
- In the T‐beam philosophy, the slab’s moment of inertia (I‐slab = b·h³/12, where b is the effective flange width) is automatically subtracted from the beam’s total inertia (I‐Tbeam) in the stiffness matrix, producing an equivalent reduced beam element. Likewise, the slab dead load over the flange width is removed to prevent double loading.  
- After the finite‐element analysis of this equivalent beam, the internal forces from the slab (moment per unit width times the flange width) are added back in automatically to yield full T‐beam internal forces. These combined moments and shears are then available for direct beam design without further manual adjustment.

Overall, Figure 2.6 illustrates both the geometric setup (centric beam in the slab mesh, with an animation offset for clarity) and the conceptual correction steps in the T‐beam method: subtract slab stiffness and load in the FE step, then reintroduce slab internal forces for structural design.

The image is labeled “Figure 2.7: Beam internal forces” and is split conceptually into a left-hand side (showing a beam–slab interaction with automatic plate‐force addition via CTRL PLAB 0) and a right-hand side (showing the pure beam forces at the FE node). A bright vertical line (drawn in green) marks the location of a support or column. A horizontal beam element (drawn in cyan and light turquoise) spans across this vertical axis, lying in the plane of a slab mesh.

1. Overall Layout

   - The beam itself is shown as a sequence of small rectangular cross-section symbols, each centered on a node of the slab mesh.

2. Left Side (CTRL PLAB 0 – Added Plate Parts)

These red shapes are labeled “beam which is connected with kinematic constraints” (above) and “beam at FE node” (above on the right side), showing how the moment distribution differs when the beam is tied by constraints versus when it is placed directly at a shell node.

4. Right Side (Beam at FE Node – Pure Beam Forces)

5. Color and Annotation Conventions

6. Purpose Illustrated  
   - The graphic compares two modeling philosophies for T-beam analysis in a slab:  
     a. Left—automatic addition of slab plate forces to the beam results via CTRL PLAB 0, yielding “T-beam” internal forces directly.  
     b. Right—pure beam analysis at FE nodes, with slab part omitted and full beam stiffness retained.  
   - It shows how kinematic constraints versus coincident node placement affect the distribution and magnitude of bending moments and shear in continuous beams embedded in slabs.

Overall, Figure 2.7 provides a side-by-side visualization of how the SOFiSTiK “T-Beam philosophy” (subtracting the slab’s I-part and dead load, then adding back slab moments) alters internal‐force diagrams compared to a standard beam‐at‐node FE model.

The illustration shows a three-dimensional, perspective view of a regular quadrilateral shell‐element mesh (representing a concrete slab) with a single straight steel beam placed “eccentrically” beneath it. Key features of the drawing are:

- Slab mesh  
  • The slab is represented as a grid of equal-sized rectangles (quad elements) drawn in light lines.  
  • The mesh is viewed at an angle so that both the top surface and part of the underside are visible.  
  • The grid extends beyond the beam in all directions, emphasizing that the beam runs across the interior of a continuous slab.

- Eccentric beam  
  • The steel beam is shown as a dashed line running diagonally from the lower-left toward the upper-right of the slab grid.  
  • It lies below the slab’s nodal plane — the beam’s centroidal axis is offset downward relative to the slab surface.  
  • The dashed style distinguishes it from plate elements and indicates that it belongs to a different element type in the finite-element model.

- Kinematic constraints  
  • At several points along the dashed beam line, small vertical connector symbols (depicted as short segments with right-angle dog-leg shapes) link the beam to the slab nodes directly above.  
  • An arrow with the label “kinematic constraint” points to one of these connector symbols. This highlights that the beam’s degrees of freedom (translations and rotations) are tied to the slab at those nodes, ensuring compatible displacements but allowing the beam to remain geometrically offset.

- Caption and numbering  
  • Below the sketch is the legend “Figure 2.8: Eccentrical defined steel beam.”  
  • This ties the graphic back to a section in the manual where different modeling philosophies (centric vs. eccentric beam definitions) and their impact on stiffness, dead load distribution, and internal‐force recovery are discussed.

Context in finite-element modeling  
- The drawing illustrates one way to model a T-beam within a slab: instead of embedding the beam in the slab plane (centric definition), the beam’s cross section is placed entirely below the slab nodes.  
- Kinematic constraints ensure that slab moments and shear forces can be transferred to the beam—a necessary step when the slab and beam elements occupy different planes.  
- This configuration triggers the program’s “eccentric T-beam philosophy,” which automatically subtracts overlapping slab stiffness and dead load, then superimposes slab moments onto the equivalent beam results for design output.  

Overall, the figure clarifies how an eccentrically positioned beam is coupled to a plate mesh in order to capture correct structural interaction without creating overlapping element volumes in the finite-element system.

The image is a three-dimensional, perspective view of a concrete slab and beam assembly modeled entirely with shell (plate) finite elements. At its core is a horizontal rectangular plate, subdivided into a regular mesh of quadrilateral shell elements. These quads cover the top surface in a grid pattern—five elements along one direction and eight along the other—creating a checkerboard-like tapestry of flat panels. Each panel represents a portion of the slab’s finite-element mesh, carrying its geometry, thickness, and stiffness.

Beneath this horizontal slab mesh, three sets of vertical shell panels extend downward along lines corresponding to the beam locations. Each vertical panel is itself subdivided into quadrilateral shell elements—four in the horizontal direction (matching the mesh above) and three in the vertical direction—so that the beam web is modeled with the same element family as the slab. These vertical panels form rectangular “curtains” of shell elements that emerge from the bottom surface of the slab, illustrating how the beam web can be cast as shell elements rather than as a separate beam element. Where each vertical curtain meets the slab, there is a conforming mesh so that nodes coincide and no duplicate volume is defined. The slab-web intersection is seamless in the finite-element sense—the plate elements share common nodes at the junction, ensuring kinematic compatibility and a single, unified stiffness matrix.

In the drawing, the horizontal slab sits at the top of the frame. Its regular element layout is clearly visible: each quad is outlined by bold edges, and the entire plate is tilted back so you see both its top face and its underside. The three vertical webs are positioned at equal intervals along the slab’s width, corresponding to supporting beams under the slab. Each web extends straight down, perpendicular to the slab plane, and retains the same shell thickness as the slab or potentially a different thickness if specified. The figure caption, “Figure 2.9: Shell elements,” labels the illustration and anchors it in the surrounding text, which discusses modeling options for T-beams within concrete slabs using shell versus beam elements.

This simply rendered but precise graphic exemplifies the second of three methods described for capturing T-beam behavior in a finite-element model: using shell (quad) elements for the web. It highlights the intersection of plate and web without volumetric overlap and shows how normal forces, shear, and bending can be resolved in a unified shell formulation. Because each element is a flat plate, designers can assign distinct thicknesses or material properties to the slab and the web panels, enabling the model to reflect a haunched slab or a composite section with minimal data duplication.

The diagram is a simplified perspective view of what SOFiSTiK calls an “eccentrical plate element,” shown in Figure 2.10 of the manual.  It combines a regular plate (slab) mesh made of QUAD elements with a local thickening below a straight beam to simulate a T-beam or haunched slab without explicitly modeling a separate beam.  Key graphical features and annotations include:

1. Mesh of Quadrilateral Plate Elements  
   - The top portion of the drawing is a rectangular grid of thin plate elements drawn as wireframe QUADs.  
   - Each QUAD is outlined by four straight lines and has a small circle plotted at each corner, indicating the “plane nodes” of the plate.  
   - Six QUADs run in the transverse direction and three in the longitudinal direction, giving a 6×3 array.  

2. Eccentrical Thickened Plate (Haunch)  
   - Directly beneath the central column of QUADs, one of the mesh panels is shown with a much greater out-of-plane thickness.  
   - The thickened region is rendered as a solid block extending downwards, representing the additional web depth of the T-beam or haunch.  
   - This protrusion aligns with the beam’s centroid line but is offset (eccentric) relative to the original slab mid-plane.  

3. Eccentricity Annotation  
   - At the left end of the beam trace, a double-headed bracket labeled “eccentricity” marks the horizontal offset between the beam’s centroid line and the plate’s node plane.  
   - A dashed horizontal line just below the plate runs the length of the mesh; this is the “centroid line below the slab,” the reference axis for beam elements.  

4. Underside of the QUAD Elements  
   - Beneath the entire slab mesh, dashed lines fan out from the corner nodes of the QUADs toward the underside of the slab.  
   - A label “underside of the QUAD elements” points to these dashed lines, emphasizing the plate’s lower surface.  

5. Plane Nodes and Centroid Line  
   - At the right-hand side of the view, a callout arrow identifies one of the circular corner nodes as a “plane node.”  
   - The centroid line below the slab is indicated by a short dashed line segment with a label pointing to it.  
   - These annotations underscore how beam elements connect at nodes in the plate plane but have their neutral axis displaced downward when the plate thickens locally.  

6. Geometric Relationships  
   - All beam elements (not explicitly drawn as beams here) would lie along the centroid line under the QUAD mesh.  
   - The eccentric plate elements share the same upper surface (the slab soffit) as the regular QUADs, but their lower surface drops to provide fiber depth for bending and shear.  
   - The sketch highlights that only the plate thickness is varied; no separate 1D beam elements are inserted.  

7. Caption and Figure Number  
   - Underneath the graphic is the caption “Figure 2.10: Eccentrical plate element,” centered and in bold, indicating its place in the documentation.  

Overall, this illustration conveys how SOFiSTiK’s eccentric plate technique creates a composite T-beam action by thickening shell elements locally under beam centrelines, while maintaining a single unified finite-element mesh. The inset labels (“eccentricity,” “underside of the QUAD elements,” “plane node,” and “centroid line below the slab”) guide the user in understanding how the mesh, beam neutral axis, and local thickening relate in space.

For their definition it is most important to take into account that the Winkler coefficient is not a simple material property but depends on the system dimensions and the loading. The Winkler coefficient defines the stress caused by a given deformation whereas the influence of adjacent points (shear deformations) is not taken into account. The dimension of a bedding is therefore given as kN/m3. A displacement causes a stress (kN/m2).
 However, the pile bedding is defined in kN/m2 since the pile ”width” has to be integrated into this value. In this case, a displacement causes a load (kN/m). Since the pile width influences also the Winkler coefficient, the pile dimensions are dropped possibly from the equation and the pile Winkler coefficient can be estimated also from the elastic modulus of the soil and a form factor.
 For circular pile cross sections and a Poisson’s ratio of 0.4 a form factor of 1.12 can be derived. For a Poisson’s ratio of 0.0 the form factor would be 1.57. In EBK 82 of the Road Traffic Department in Rheinland-Pfalz the extreme values of the form factor are scheduled to be 0.5 and 2.0.
 Simplifying to DIN 4014 a foundation modulus ks = Es/D (at D > 1.0m D = 1.0m may be used) can be determined. For the input, the user has to multiply this value with D because SOFiSTiK requires a beam bedding input k = D · ks as line-shaped foundation per m pile length.

In general, the set of differential equations can not be solved directly. Therefore, for each pile, these equations are integrated numerically by the Runge-Kutta method. The step width is con- trolled automatically to maintain a relative accuracy of 0.01 percent. The setting of higher error limits results in a reduction of the CPU time. The setting of smaller error limits is reasonable up to a certain value, which depends on the machine accuracy of the computer used. The reduc- tion of the error limit below a certain value is not reasonable because the computational error
 increases again due to the rounding errors in the high number of the necessary additions.
 In the case of an unbedded beam the step width can be set very large. By contrast, for large Winkler coefficients the numerical calculation becomes more difficult. As a criterion the characteristic length is used, defined as:
 L= V4-EI/K

 This value is an estimation of the distance between the zero points of the solution function. For reasons with reference to the numerical integration, the characteristic length should not become less than 1/5 up to 1/10 of the element length. If this condition is not satisfied, great accuracy problems may occur resulting in differential forces in the nodes which are pointed out in an error message.
 These problems can be overcome by subdividing a pile into more subelements.
 In the case that a pile is subdivided into more elements, the placing of the nodes at points of changing soil parameters (layers) is to be preferred over an uniform subdivision.

The illustration, titled “Figure 2.18: Spring force‐displacement diagrams,” is composed of three side-by-side Cartesian plots.  Each plot shares the same pair of orthogonal axes:  
  • Horizontal axis, labeled “V,” represents spring displacement (positive to the right).  
  • Vertical axis, labeled “P,” represents spring force (positive upward).  

All curves are drawn as bold black piecewise lines on a white background, with certain threshold distances or force levels marked by small double‐headed arrows and textual labels.  No colors or shading are used; the emphasis is strictly on the geometry of each force–displacement relationship.

1. Leftmost Plot (Gap Spring)  
   – Region near the origin: a horizontal line segment of zero slope spans a finite displacement interval on either side of V = 0, indicating a “dead zone” in which no force is generated.  At each end of this flat segment small outward‐pointing arrows are annotated “GAP,” signifying the gap width (i.e. the displacement that must be exceeded before the spring engages).  
   – For V greater than the positive gap threshold, a straight line with positive slope rises from the end of the flat zone, denoting a linear spring behavior beyond the gap.  
   – For V less than the negative gap threshold, a straight line with the same (or in some model variants a different) slope extends downward and leftward, indicating symmetric spring action in compression once the gap is closed.  

2. Center Plot (Compression-Only Gap or Crack-Reopening Spring)  
   – A continuous straight line of constant positive slope passes through the origin, covering the tensile (positive V) side, indicating an always-active linear spring under tension.  
   – On the compression (negative V) side, a horizontal “dead” band exists immediately adjacent to the origin.  This zero-force segment is marked by a small arrow labeled “CRA,” which stands for crack-reopening allowance or compression release allowance.  It indicates that the spring does not resist a small amount of compression until the displacement exceeds this CRA threshold.  
   – Beyond the negative threshold, the linear spring law resumes with the same slope as in tension.  

3. Rightmost Plot (Yielding Spring)  
   – A straight line of constant slope emanates from the origin in both tension and compression regions, up to a finite force level on each side.  
   – Small double‐headed arrows placed just above and below the origin on the P axis are labeled “YIELD,” pinpointing the force magnitude at which the spring transitions from elastic behavior into plastic or yielded behavior.  
   – Once the force reaches this yield level (either positive or negative), further displacement is accommodated by a horizontal plateau: the curve flattens, indicating that additional displacement occurs at essentially constant force (plastic flow or slip).  

Together, these three sketches exemplify common non‐linear spring element phenomena encountered in advanced structural analyses: clearance gaps, crack‐closure effects, and material yielding.  The figure directly supports the surrounding text’s discussion of how non‐linear springs may be defined in terms of displacement thresholds (gaps), lateral friction and cohesion, prestress effects, and work laws with hysteresis.

The image is a two‐part schematic comparing the deformation capabilities of a “conforming” 4-node quadrilateral element (QTYP 0) versus a “nonconforming” 4-node element augmented with internal quadratic shape functions (QTYP 1). Both parts are drawn in red, and each is surrounded by black straight arrows (membrane forces) and red curved arrows (disc bending moments) to illustrate the identical loading in each case. A short caption beneath reads:  
“element QTYP 0, bottom QTYP 1 with intern nonconforming shape functions.”

1. Top diagram (QTYP 0, conforming bilinear element)  
 • The element is shown as a simple quadrilateral with four straight edges. In this depiction its top and bottom edges are parallel, and the left and right edges are straight but slightly inclined—yielding a trapezoidal overall form under load.  
 • Two horizontal black arrows flank it: on the left side a black arrow points into the element, on the right side one points outward. These represent a constant in-plane bending disc moment enforced via paired membrane forces.  
 • At each of the element’s four corners a red curved arrow indicates the applied bending moment.  
 • Under this load the element deforms to another straight-edged quadrilateral (still purely bilinear interpolation of displacements and rotations), which can only capture a uniform variation of shear force and bending moment. Because all displacement and rotation fields remain continuous across elements (“conforming”), there is no jump at element interfaces—but the linear interpolation induces significant shear deformation energy. The result is an overly stiff response, incapable of representing pure bending without spurious shear.

2. Bottom diagram (QTYP 1, nonconforming element with internal quadratic functions)  
 • The element is again sketched in red, but now each of its four boundaries is slightly curved: the top edge bows inward (concave), the bottom bows outward (convex), and the sides bow outward as well. This curvature is the visible signature of the additional internal (non-nodal) shape functions, which are zero at the corner nodes but nonzero throughout the element interior.  
 • The same pair of horizontal black arrows at mid-sides (one pointing in, one pointing out) and the same red curved arrows at the corners indicate identical loading as in the top figure.  
 • Under these conditions, the QTYP 1 element can exactly reproduce the pure bending deformation—its curved geometry absorbs the loading without incurring shear strains. As a result, it achieves the correct stiffness for in-plane bending, whereas QTYP 0 cannot.

Overall, this side-by-side shows why the default QTYP 1 nonconforming element (with six internal quadratic functions as per Hughes & Tezduyar or Wilson) is preferred in ASE: it can capture linear moment variations (exactly in rectangular cases, approximately in general quadrilaterals) and avoids artificial stiffness from shear locking by sacrificing strict inter-element displacement continuity.

The 4-node element with QTYP-0 is characterised through only bilinear accretion of the dis- placements and rotations. This accretion describes a uniform variation of the shear force and of the bending moment via a transformation. This element is called conforming, because the displacements and the rotations between elements do not have any jumps. The results at the gravity centre of the element represent the actual internal force variation fairly well, whilst the results at the corners are relatively useless, especially the ones at the edges or at the corners of a region.
 Taylor and Wilson came up with the idea to describe more stress states through additional func- tions that value is zero at all nodes. As a rule, these functions lead to a substantial improvement of the results, however, they violate the continuity of displacements between elements. Thus
 they are called non-conforming elements.
 On the example of a membrane action the effect or the nonconforming shape functions can be clarified best. In fig. 2.21 on top we see an element with QTYP 0 forced with a constand inplane bending disc moment, applied with two pairs of membrane forces. The linear shape functions only allow the plotted displacement. The high shear deformations attract a lot of energy and so the element is much to stiff for this action.
 On the bottom an element with nonconforming quadratic intern shape functions is shown. This element can represent this action exactly without shear deformations and delivers a correct stiffness.
 In ASE the more powerful QTYP 1 element is the default. With CTRL option QTYP the simple element can be selected for special test cases.

Context and implications:

- By default (e.g. linear or purely quadratic BRICs), only edge‐based quadratic shape functions are active, which suffice to represent uniform bending exactly in hex-elements.  
- The “v4” variants let you step up to higher‐order p-enrichments for educational purposes or special contact regions, as controlled further by the CTRL V5 command.  
- No face modes are available in v4 1–2, so these behave like classical non-conforming BRICs (edge polynomial only). Starting at v4 3, face modes of polynomial degree 2 supplement the edge modes, improving representation of bending and membrane behavior without refining the mesh.  
- The number of Gauss points grows along with polynomial degree to ensure exact integration: 5 points for quadratic‐only, 11 for cubic, 14 for quartic, and 24 for quintic plus quadratic faces.  
- Although higher p-modes can be invoked, typical practice—especially when working with PLC primary loadcases—is to stick with quadratic edge enrichment due to limited database storage and marginal accuracy gains beyond that. Mesh refinement is recommended instead of p-escalation for most production runs.

The image is a two-dimensional yield locus plot (Figure 2.24) for concrete governed by the LADE material law under biaxial loading. It shows, in the σx–σy plane, the combinations of principal stresses at which the concrete transitions from elastic to inelastic (yielding or cracking) behavior. Key features of the plot and its annotation are:

Axes and Sign Convention  
 • Horizontal axis: σx [MPa], arrow pointing to the right.  
 • Vertical axis: σy [MPa], arrow pointing upward.  
 • Zero stress is placed at the origin (0,0). Ticks along both axes are labeled –20.0 and –40.0, indicating that compressive stress is taken as negative. Thus, moving left or downward from the origin increases compressive magnitude.  

Curve Geometry  
 • A single, closed blue curve traces out the limit surface in the negative quadrant (compressive–compressive domain), bulging outward from the axes and returning to the origin.  
 • The topmost point of the curve lies on the σy axis, marking the biaxial stress state at which pure σy compression alone reaches its limit.  
 • The rightmost (in modulus) point on the curve lies on the σx axis, marking the maximum uniaxial compressive strength in the x-direction.  
 • Between these intercepts, the locus bows smoothly, representing the reduction in allowable σy as σx increases in compression (and vice versa).  

Numerical Annotation  
 • In the figure caption below the plot one reads: “Yield curve Lade mno: 30 uniaxial sigmax = –38.0.”  
   – “mno = 30” refers to a parameter in the LADE model that shapes the yield surface curvature.  
   – “uniaxial sigmax = –38.0 MPa” identifies the maximum compressive stress in the x-direction under uniaxial loading.  
 • By symmetry of the LADE model in pure compression, the uniaxial strength in the y-direction is the same magnitude, even though only the σx value is explicitly stated.  

Interpretation in Context  
 • This yield curve is used during finite-element analyses with BRIC volume elements (8-node hexahedra) or tetrahedral elements with quadratic edge modes.  
 • In mesh-based simulations of concrete structures (e.g. tunnel linings, slabs, beams), the LADE law defines when and how the material begins to crack or yield under combined σx–σy loading.  
 • The shape of the curve reflects concrete’s characteristic behavior: it sustains higher combined biaxial compression than pure uniaxial compression (the bulged middle region), but its tensile capacity (positive stresses) is effectively zero, so the locus closes at the origin on the tension side.  

Overall, the plot succinctly encapsulates the biaxial strength envelope for concrete under the LADE material law. It provides engineers and simulation software with the critical boundary between elastic and inelastic behavior when concrete is subjected to simultaneous stresses in two principal directions.

The image is a line-plot of three standard concrete stress–strain curves generated by the AQUA pre-processor (and echoed in ASE when ECHO MAT YES is set). The vertical axis is labeled in megapascal [MPa], running from 0 at the origin down to –35 MPa (compression). The horizontal axis is labeled in parts per thousand [‰] (strain), from 0.0 on the left to –3.50 on the right. Five fine dashed vertical grid-lines mark key strain values at approximately –1.10 ‰, –2.00 ‰, –2.20 ‰, –3.30 ‰ and –3.50 ‰; these correspond to characteristic limit-state strains (e.g. cracking, ultimate, and post-peak deformations).

Three distinct curves are plotted and color-coded:

  • A green curve (sig-m) rises steeply from the origin to a peak compressive stress of roughly –32 MPa at about –2.20 ‰ strain. Beyond the peak it gently descends toward –27 MPa at –3.50 ‰, representing the non-linear stress–strain law used in deformation (serviceability) analysis.  
  • A red curve (sig-u) follows a smoother, parabola-rectangle shape, peaking around –18 MPa at roughly –1.80 ‰ strain, then flattening into a plateau out to –3.50 ‰. This is the stress–strain diagram applied in cross-section (ultimate) design.  
  • A blue curve (sig-r) is the lowest of the three, peaking near –15 MPa around –2.00 ‰ strain before gradually declining to about –13 MPa at –3.50 ‰. It represents the non-linear material law for determination of internal forces and moments.

Each curve is labeled in small text adjacent to its upper branch (“sig-m” in green near the highest curve, “sig-u” in red in the middle, “sig-r” in blue at the bottom). The plot’s title or caption (partially visible below the figure) reads: “AQUA plot of the standard stress-strain curves for concrete.”

In the context of ASE/AQUA workflows, these three curves correspond to the definitions selectable via record NSTR (items KSV for concrete and KSB for reinforcement, though here only concrete curves are shown). When the option ECHO MAT YES is active in ASE, the actual curves used in the calculation—sig-u for ultimate‐limit‐state design, sig-r for internal‐force analysis, and sig-m for deformation/serviceability checks—are printed and graphed exactly as seen here. The dashed vertical lines align with the strain points entered in SSLA records (e.g., points defining the transition from tensile to compressive branches and the ultimate strain), making it straightforward to verify that safety coefficients, splines, and other input parameters (EPS, SIG, TYPE) have been applied correctly. This graphical output enhances transparency by showing engineers which stress–strain relationships are driving crack‐width predictions, tension‐stiffening models, and non‐linear material behavior in reinforced‐concrete analyses.

The vertical axis on the left is labeled “[MPa]” and carries major tick marks at 100 MPa intervals, ranging from +700 MPa at the top down to –700 MPa at the bottom. Three piece-wise-linear curves rise steeply from the origin in the elastic range (between 0 and ±2.75 o/oo) and then flatten into nearly horizontal plateaus in the plastic range (from ±2.75 o/oo out to ±25 o/oo):

content:
The input table establishes a clear mapping between the three “families” of stress–strain curves used in concrete and reinforcement modeling and the keywords by which they are defined in AQUA (via the SSLA record) and selected in ASE (via the NSTR record).  Below is a detailed breakdown of each column and row in that table, together with how it ties into the surrounding workflow.  

1. Column headings  
   • “Designation of the stress-strain curve”  
     – Identifies the name, colour (for plotting) and primary application of each curve.  
   • “Type in AQUA record SSLA”  
     – Gives the exact SSLA keyword (the TYPE value) to be used when defining a curve in AQUA.  
   • “Selection in ASE NSTR without/with safety coefficient”  
     – Lists the two-letter codes that ASE expects in its NSTR record (KSV or KSB) to pick the curve, first for the raw curve (no partial-safety factor applied) and second for the factored curve (with the default safety coefficient from the AQUA definition).  

2. Row-by-row description  

   a. sig-u (red): design curve (“parabola-rectangle” cross-section design)  
      • Colour: red (used in plots)  
      • Purpose: ultimate‐limit‐state design of concrete cross sections, based on the standard parabola–rectangle stress distribution  
      • AQUA SSLA TYPE keyword: ULTI  
      • ASE NSTR selection codes:  
        – “UL” = use the raw (unfactored) ULTI curve  
        – “ULD” = use ULTI with the safety coefficient defined in SSLA (e.g. 1.3)  

   b. sig-r (blue): non-linear analysis of internal forces and moments  
      • Colour: blue  
      • Purpose: refine internal‐force and moment results under non-linear concrete behaviour  
      • AQUA SSLA TYPE keyword: CALC  
      • ASE NSTR selection codes:  
        – “CAL” = CALC curve without safety factor  
        – “CALD” = CALC curve factored by the SSLA safety coefficient  

   c. sig-m (green): non-linear deformation analysis  
      • Colour: green  
      • Purpose: accurately capture deformations, crack widths and tension stiffening in serviceability‐limit‐state checks  
      • AQUA SSLA TYPE keyword: SERV  
      • ASE NSTR selection codes:  
        – “SL” = SERV curve un-factored  
        – “SLD” = SERV curve with safety factor from SSLA  

3. How this fits into the ASE–AQUA workflow  
   • Defining curves in AQUA:  
     – A pair of SSLA records (one each for concrete tensile and compressive branches, or steel) specify EPS, SIG and TYPE plus any intermediate points (with “spl” for spline).  
     – The numeric value following TYPE (e.g. “SERV 1.3”) sets the partial‐safety coefficient.  
   • Selecting curves in ASE:  
     – In the NSTR record, KSV chooses the concrete curve; KSB (if present) chooses the reinforcement curve.  
     – You may combine any concrete and steel curves arbitrarily by specifying both KSV and KSB.  
     – Append “D” to the code (ULD, CALD, SLD) to engage the safety factor defined back in AQUA.  
   • Transparency and checking:  
     – Set “ECHO MAT YES” in ASE so that the actually used stress–strain curves and all material parameters (FCT, FCK, crack‐width control, tension‐stiffening method, etc.) are printed in the URSULA/ASE output.  
     – The output will also include plots of all three curves (red, blue, green) and a detailed tensile‐zone graph.  

In summary, this table serves as a quick‐reference legend linking the conceptual curve names (sig-u, sig-r, sig-m) with the precise keywords needed in AQUA (SSLA) and the two-letter selectors (with or without the “D” suffix) needed in ASE’s NSTR record, ensuring consistency across definition, selection, plotting and safety‐factor application.

The illustration (labeled “Figure 2.34: Heterogeneous Layers”) presents a simplified, two-dimensional cross-section of a three-layer composite element—specifically a glass–plastic–glass laminate. Shown as a long, horizontal bar, the section is divided into three parallel strata:

• Top layer: a narrow band colored in cyan/turquoise with the label “glass” positioned above it.  
• Middle layer: a thicker band colored in a paler aqua or mint-green, centrally located and labeled “plastic.”  
• Bottom layer: a mirror of the top band, also colored in cyan/turquoise and bearing the same “glass” label below it.

Visually, the outer glass layers are of equal thickness, framing the central plastic layer, which is noticeably thicker. The color contrast between the bright outer bands and the lighter central band serves to emphasize the material heterogeneity. The graphic uses clean, solid fills and simple black text labels, without any additional textures or shading. There are no dimension lines or numerical thickness values shown directly on the figure—its purpose is purely schematic, to convey the idea of layered construction rather than provide exact measurements.

Contextually within the surrounding text, this figure exemplifies how a laminated composite (glass–plastic–glass) can be defined in a finite-element preprocessor (AQUA) for later use in a non-linear analysis program (ASE). It illustrates the concept behind the FLAY command, which allows the user to stack layers of different materials—each previously defined under its own material number—into a single QUAD element. In this example:  
– Material 11 is used for the glass layers (each 6 mm thick).  
– Material 12 is used for the plastic interlayer (3 mm thick).  
By arranging these layers in the input deck with successive T (thickness) and material-number entries under a FLAY record, the user creates a composite cross-section whose overall bending-stiffness, shear-stiffness, and other orthotropic properties are captured in the resulting 8×8 material matrix (D) printed by ASE.

Although the figure itself does not show numeric values or element boundaries, it visually underscores the notion of “heterogeneous layers” in laminated plates. In practice, this model is suitable for global, plate-theory analyses—where each layer remains planar and no inter-layer slip is assumed—but is not intended for detailed study of local delamination or coupling-point failures, which would require three-dimensional volume elements and explicit interface modeling.

   - From the bottom left corner arrow on the left square, a curved arrow sweeps to the bottom left corner of the right square, carrying the text: “Node force from element stress of the PLC: FACL.”

   - Inside the square, the same double-headed vertical arrow appears, indicating the element’s expansion or preferred deformation under the adopted primary stress FACP.

Purpose and Context (how it ties back to bending/shear discussion)  
   - This drawing concretely illustrates how, in a staged construction analysis, the internally generated stresses from a primary loadcase must be re-applied in the subsequent loadcase—even if no new external loads are added—in order to maintain equilibrium.  
   - The node forces (FACL) and element stresses (FACP) derived from the PLC effectively become “expansion loads” that counteract the continued external loads, mirroring the algorithmic approach described for layered plate bending, shear stiffness summation, and the treatment of pre‐stress and creep factors.

The figure is a schematic uniaxial stress–strain diagram divided into three distinct regions and annotated with the key points and parameters that define elastic behavior, yielding and strain-hardening. It is intended to illustrate how the stress in a material evolves under increasing uniaxial tensile strain, and it carries the caption “Figure 2.37: Uniaxial stress.”

1. Axes and Overall Layout  
 - The vertical axis is labeled “STRESS” and runs upward from zero at the origin.  
 - The horizontal axis is labeled “EPSY” (representing the total uniaxial strain) and extends to the right from zero at the origin.  
 - Two vertical grid lines are drawn at specific strain values on the horizontal axis, marking eps-e (the elastic limit strain) and eps-z (the strain at which the material reaches its ultimate stress or onset of necking).  
 - Above each of these vertical grid lines the corresponding stress levels (beta-e and beta-u) are indicated by small horizontal “T”-shaped markers.

2. Region I: Linear Elastic Behavior (0 ≤ ε ≤ εₑ)  
 - Starting at the origin (zero stress, zero strain), the stress–strain curve follows a straight line with a constant slope. This slope corresponds to the elastic modulus E, consistent with σ = E·ε in the purely elastic range.  
 - The endpoint of this linear segment is at ε = εₑ on the horizontal axis, where the stress has reached σ = βₑ (the elastic limit stress or yield stress). At this point the material transitions from purely elastic deformation into the onset of yield.

3. Region II: Yield Plateau or Reduced Hardening (εₑ ≤ ε ≤ ε𝑧)  
 - Immediately beyond εₑ, the curve changes slope dramatically: it becomes flatter, indicating that further increases in strain produce only small additional increases in stress. This region represents plastic flow or yielding in which the material is deforming plastically under near-constant or slowly rising stress.  
 - The stress in this mid-region rises gradually from βₑ at εₑ up toward a higher plateau value βᵤ at ε𝑧. The gentle incline models strain hardening, where dislocation motion becomes progressively more difficult as plastic deformation proceeds.

4. Region III: Ultimate Stress Plateau (ε ≥ ε𝑧)  
 - At ε = ε𝑧 on the horizontal axis, the stress reaches its maximum plateau value denoted “be” (sometimes referred to as βᵤ or the ultimate tensile stress).  
 - For strains beyond ε𝑧, the curve becomes essentially horizontal, indicating that further straining does not increase the nominal stress—the material has reached its maximum load-carrying capacity and may be entering necking or stable plastic flow without additional hardening.

5. Key Notations and Interpretation  
 - εₑ (“eps-e”) marks the elastic limit or the onset of permanent plastic deformation.  
 - ε𝑧 (“eps-z”) marks the strain at which the material reaches its ultimate tensile stress and strain-hardening ceases.  
 - βₑ (“beta-e”) is the stress at the elastic limit; βᵤ or “be” is the ultimate or plateau stress.  
 - The three-segment, piecewise-linear approximation is commonly used in structural and finite-element codes to capture (a) linear elasticity, (b) yielding with reduced stiffness, and (c) a final plastic plateau.  

6. Relation to Creep, Pre-stress and Combined Loading (Contextual Notes)  
 - Although the diagram itself shows only monotonic uniaxial loading, the surrounding text explains how primary stresses, creep factors (FCREEP1, FCREEP2), pre-stress records (GRP-PREX) and temperature or expansion loads (ε,LOAD) can be superimposed on such a curve in a multilayer plate or sandwich element.  
 - In a full nonlinear analysis, the stress–strain law would be combined with the Steiner terms for eccentric layer centroids, orthotropic restrictions and plasticisation numbers (ƒ = (σlinear – fᵧ)/fᵧ) to assess yielding under combined normal and shear stresses.  
 - The figure therefore serves as the basis for constructing the stress–strain matrix D of each layer and for integrating stresses through the thickness when computing bending moments, shear stresses and nodal loads in a plate or shell formulation.

The figure (numbered “2.38”) is a black-and-white plot entitled “Biaxial failure curve according to Kupfer-Hilsdorf-Ruesch.” It presents a two-dimensional failure envelope for concrete under combined principal stresses, normalized by the concrete’s uniaxial compressive strength βc.  

1. Axes and Scales  
 • Horizontal axis: σ₁/|βc|, running from –1.2 at the left through 0 at the center to +0.2 at the right in increments of 0.2.  
 • Vertical axis: σ₂/|βc|, running from –1.2 at the bottom through 0 at the center to +0.2 at the top in the same increments.  
 • Both axes are drawn with arrowheads at their positive ends; the origin (0,0) lies at the geometric center of the drawing.  

2. Failure Envelope  
 • A closed, lobed curve encloses the region of safe stress combinations. Its shape is roughly square but bulges outward more strongly in the compressive quadrant (negative σ₁ and σ₂).  
 • The boundary is drawn as a thick continuous line, denoting the limit between elastic and failure states under biaxial loading.  
 • Along this envelope, numerous small arrows indicate the direction of increasing biaxial loading paths (i.e., how stress states traverse toward failure).  

3. Radial Stress‐Ratio Lines  
 • From the origin, three straight radial lines extend into the compressive quadrant. Each is labeled with a constitutive ratio:  
   – “σ₁ = σ₂” (45° line into quadrant III)  
   – “σ₁ = 0.52 σ₂” (a shallower line)  
   – “σ₁ = 0.22 σ₂” (an even shallower line)  
 • These lines illustrate particular proportional biaxial loading cases used in deriving the envelope.  

4. Inset 3D Sketch of a Concrete Cube  
 • To the lower left of the envelope is a small three‐dimensional sketch of a 5 cm‐edged cube.  
 • One face of the cube is marked σ₁ (horizontal arrow), and the adjacent orthogonal face is marked σ₂ (vertical arrow).  
 • This inset conveys the physical meaning of the two principal stresses acting on orthogonal faces of the concrete element.  

5. Noteworthy Observations  
 • Almost the entire failure curve lies in the negative‐negative quadrant, emphasizing that concrete is much weaker in tension (positive values) than in compression.  
 • The envelope’s slight “corner” toward the positive axes shows a very limited tensile biaxial capacity.  
 • The curve is smooth with no sharp corners, reflecting a continuous failure criterion based on principal stress combinations rather than discrete yield points.  

Overall, the graphic provides a compact visualization of how concrete’s compressive strength degrades under simultaneous biaxial stress states, as formulated by Kupfer, Hilsdorf, and Ruesch. It combines both the theoretical failure locus in normalized stress space and a small physical model that helps interpret the two‐axis loading scenario on a concrete specimen.

The image is a simplified two-dimensional plot of a uniaxial tensile stress-strain law for plain concrete in the “tensile zone,” reproduced as Figure 2.39. It consists of a pair of orthogonal axes: the horizontal axis, labeled “eps” (strain), increases to the right; the vertical axis, labeled “sigma” (stress), increases upward. 

Starting at the origin (0, 0), the stress–strain relationship rises along a straight, positive-sloped line until it reaches a distinct “cracking point.” This point is marked by a small vertical tic at a strain value designated “epslin” on the horizontal axis. At that strain, the corresponding maximum tensile stress is labeled “beta-z.” Graphically, the ascending branch is drawn as a heavy line segment directly connecting the origin with (epslin, beta-z).

Beyond epslin, the concrete is assumed to have cracked; the stress begins to decrease with further increase in strain. A second straight line slopes downward from the peak (epslin, beta-z) to a terminal point on the strain axis where the stress returns to zero. The endpoint’s strain coordinate is not explicitly labeled but lies to the right of epslin.  

The area under this descending branch and above the horizontal axis is filled with parallel diagonal hatching and marked “GF.” This shaded triangular region graphically represents the tensile fracture energy (denoted GF or G_F in the accompanying text), i.e. the energy required to propagate a crack per unit area.  

Beneath the entire diagram appears the caption “Figure 2.39: Uniaxial stress-strain curve for the tensile zone,” indicating that this is the program-internal constitutive law used by ASE for modeling the softening behavior of concrete once cracking initiates.  

In context, epslin corresponds to the strain at which concrete reaches its lower fractile tensile stiffness (fctk) and begins to crack. The tensile strength at cracking is taken as beta-z, and the triangular softening branch quantitatively distributes the fracture energy GF over increasing crack opening (strain), typically limited by a control parameter (CTRL CONC VAL) to prevent excessive post-peak lengthening.  

Overall, the figure neatly encapsulates: 
 • The elastic-brittle ascending branch up to cracking (linear up to epslin, at stress beta-z)  
 • A linear softening branch from the cracking point to zero stress at a higher strain  
 • The fracture energy GF shaded beneath the softening curve.  

As described in the surrounding text, if a user has already defined a tensile stress-strain curve in AQUA, that curve will override this internal default; otherwise, ASE generates this triangular stress‐strain law to capture tension stiffening effects, crack propagation, and post-peak softening in reinforced or plain concrete elements.

The image is a schematic stress–strain diagram of reinforcing steel in tension, overlaid with the “tension‐stiffening” modification according to DAfStb‐Heft 525 (picture H 8-4) and Heft 600 (picture H5-11). It is intended to illustrate how the basic steel stress–strain law is adapted to account for the residual bond and crack‐bridging action of concrete between cracks. The key features and annotations are as follows:

1. Coordinate Axes  
   • Horizontal axis: εs (steel strain) increasing from left (zero) to right.  
   • Vertical axis: σs (steel stress) increasing from bottom (zero) to top.

2. Basic Steel Stress–Strain Backbone (black line)  
   • Begins at the origin (0,0) with an initial small “zig-zag” representing a residual steel stress σsr at the first crack strain εsr1.  
   • Rises linearly from εsr1 to a point labeled εsmy, reaching the usual yield stress fy.  
   • A horizontal plastic plateau at fy continues until the upper yield strain εsy or minimum of εsmy (mean steel strain).  
   • Beyond yield, the curve slopes upward again (strain hardening) until a maximum steel strain εsmu; finally it flattens out at ultimate strength and ultimate strain εsu.

3. Tension-Stiffening Modification (red line)  
   • Overlaid on the basic backbone to show the increased apparent tensile capacity of the steel–concrete composite after cracking.  
   • From εsr1 it rises more steeply than the basic steel law, passing through two highlighted “red‐circled” points: the first at the residual stress level σsr and the second near yielding.  
   • Between these two circled points the slope is enhanced by a factor βt, indicated graphically by an arrow labeled βt·(εsr2 – εsr1). This factor represents the additional strain carried by the concrete “process zone” LZ.  
   • Past the second circled point, the red curve rejoins the basic steel backbone at exactly εsmy, then follows the same plastic and hardening branches to ultimate.

4. Annotations of Characteristic Strains  
   • εsr1: first‐crack strain, where concrete first loses tensile capacity and steel picks up the load.  
   • εsr2: second marker used for defining the tension‐stiffening interval.  
   • εsmy: mean yield strain (start of full yielding in reinforced‐concrete serviceability analysis).  
   • εsy: characteristic yield strain of steel.  
   • εsmu and εsu: strain limits for strain hardening and ultimate capacity.

5. Interval I and Interval II (green and blue arrows below the main graph)  
   • A small green triangle is drawn beneath the origin of the plot, its apex indicating the first interval “I.” A blue arrow marks the transition from I to II.  
   • Interval I covers linear elastic tension of the cracked composite (steel + bonded concrete).  
   • Interval II covers the post‐crack, tension‐stiffening range until steel yield.

6. Caption Text  
   • Below the figure reads: “Tensile stiffening acc. to Heft 525 picture H 8-4 and Heft 600 picture H5-11.”

Overall, the illustration demonstrates how ASE (the finite‐element concrete analysis module) modifies the pure‐steel stress–strain curve in serviceability and ultimate limit states to include the additional tensile resistance provided by concrete “between cracks.” The red line quantifies the enhanced slope and stress levels up to steel yield (εsmy), controlled by the process‐zone length LZ, fracture energy GF, and lower fractile tension stiffness fctk, all of which appear in the user‐defined parameters (e.g., CTRL CONC V3, V4, etc.).
