Examples see ase.dat\...\nonlinear_quad\ a1_introduction_example.dat The following litera- ture was consulted on the concrete material law: Stempniewski and Eibl [11], Feenstra and De Borst [12], and Schiessel [13]
 Following current assessments and explanations are mentioned here additionally: xx [14], Zilch and Rogge [15], Bellmann and Rötzer [16], xx [17], and Schneider [18]
 The material behaviour of reinforced concrete can be described by the following properties:
 • Non-linear stress-strain curve in tension and compressive zone
 • Contribution of the concrete between cracks (tension stiffening)
 • Non-linear material behaviour of the steel inserts
 • Simplified check of the plate’s shear stress
 • ASE performs a nonlinear analysis with a given reinforcement. An increase of reinforce- ment can be controlled via REIQ-CHKR.
 Usual procedure:
 The element is subdivided into NLAY layers. The stresses sigma-x, sigma-y and tau-xy and the principal stresses sigma-I and sigma-II are calculated for every layer’s boundary. For each principal stress direction a stress-strain curve is generated, which results from the principal stress relation in the respective direction. The thus established non-linear stresses are then integrated over all the layers to find the internal forces. After this all the forces of the reinforce- ment including the tension-stiffening-effect are added. Finally an independent check is made for the plate’s shear stresses.
 The following is a list of the concrete parameters taken from record CONC:
 CONC-FC
 = calculation value of the concrete stiffness
 CONC-FCT
 = average tension stiffness for tension stiffening
 CONC-FCTK = lower fractile of the tension stiffness for bare concrete
 CONC-GC = GC compression fracture energy
 CONC-GF
 = GF tension fracture energy
 CONC-MUEC = friction value in the crack splice
 Further inputs in ASE:
 LC - BET2 = load duration coefficient (beta2)

CONC-FCTK = lower fractile of the tension stiffness for bare concrete. CONC-GC = GC compression fracture energy. CONC-GF. = GF tension fracture energy. CONC-MUEC = friction value in the crack splice. Further inputs in ASE:. LC - BET2 = load duration coefficient (beta2).
 CTRL - NLAY = number of layers to be calculated >=6,
 default = 10
 Analysis on Serviceability Stress Level
 Using the 1.0-times serviceability loads the maximum desired stress is input for this serviceabil- ity state at the material. The deformation and crack width to be expected is in this case mostly interesting. The input of the concrete tensile strength of the (pure) concrete layer is particularly important. This value is input in AQUA in CONC...FCTK and it can be modified subsequently temporarily in ASE with CTRL CONC V3+V4. The serviceability stress-strain curve without any additional material safeties is requested then in ASE (NSTR KSV SL = default).
 The selection of a realistic concrete tensile strength fctk (pure strength without reinforcement) is here very important. If fctk or CTRL CONC V4 is not input, the plate remains in uncracked
 state I. It can be therefore reasonable to decrease the value e.g. onto 60 % in order to con- sider a crack predamage from construction stage (hydration heat). On the other hand realistic deflections are resulted often only with a high initial value for fctk.
 Analysis with gamma-times Loads
 If using gamma-times loads the corresponding material stress-strain curve has to be selected in record NSTR in ASE. There are two possibilities that are also well shown in the beam example aseaqb_1_column_cracked.dat :
 • Analysis according to "non-linear method": Here an averaged material safety of 1.3 is used. The material strengths are modified for this purpose. They are available AQUA and can be requested in ASE with NSTR KSV CALD.
 • Analysis in ultimate limit state NSTR KSV ULD
 In both cases the pure concrete alone must include any tensile strengths. CTRL CONC V4 0.0 or 0.01 must be input!
 The increase of the steel stress due to the concrete action between the cracks may be brought into approach (default for fct or CTRL CONC V3).

In both cases the pure concrete alone must include any tensile strengths. CTRL CONC V4 0.0 or 0.01 must be input!. The increase of the steel stress due to the concrete action between the cracks may be brought into approach (default for fct or CTRL CONC V3)..
 A non-linear analysis for the ultimate limit state is particularly necessary for additional effects from second-order theory. Such an analysis with temporarily switched-off tensile strength of the pure concrete causes however often big deformations and bad convergences.
 A reasonable procedure is therefore often also a determination of the internal forces and mo- ments with average values of the material strengths (analysis in serviceability limit state) and a definitive design of the redistributed internal forces and moments with an average load safety coefficient (e.g. 1.45)
 Futher explanations see example a2_nonlinear_slab.dat
 Non-linear Stress-Strain Curve in the Compressive Zone
 The maximum concrete compression strength beta-ic, found in the compressive zone, is re- duced from the principal stress relation. Beta-ic can either be read from the Kupfer curve, or it can be calculated by the respective equations [ 1] , pg. 260.
 With this maximum value beta-ic an uniaxial stress-strain line can be generated according to the concrete stress-strain curve for every of both principal stress directions.
 An increase value higher than 1.0 is only allowed for calculations in serviceability limit state. For calculations with gamma-times loads (ultimate limit state) this increase is deactivated in the default, because it is mostly desired that the maximum stress increases about the basic value of the concrete compressive strength beta-ic - see CTRL CONC V2.
 A reduction of the permissible compressive stresses due to lateral tension (and lateral cracks) is taken into account and can be adapted with CTRL CONC V6. The maximum reduction is reached with a transverse tension stress of fctk (or at least -0.05*fcm) and remains on this level also on higher tensile strains.
 In case the maximum concrete compression strength is modified, the work law must be adapted. To keep the start E modulus as well as the strain for max. strength, the worklay is compressed from 0.0-1.0 permille strain and lengthened in 1.5-2.5 permille.

In case the maximum concrete compression strength is modified, the work law must be adapted. To keep the start E modulus as well as the strain for max. strength, the worklay is compressed from 0.0-1.0 permille strain and lengthened in 1.5-2.5 permille..
 In the tensile zone of concrete, the maximum value beta-z, is always taken as the lower fractile of the concrete stiffness fctk. The length of the descending curve results from the tension crack energy GF of the processing zone. Typical values lie between 0.10 and 0.25 Nmm/mm2. The program restricts the length of the descending curve to 5·epslin - see CTRL CONC VAL.
 If a stress-strain curve for concrete is already defined in the tensile zone in AQUA, then this one is used instead of the here described program-internal curve! Thus it is possible to calculated steel fibre concrete -> steel_fibre_concrete.dat
 The element is seen as cracked as soon as the tensile-strain crosses the linear limit value of epslin. Any further strain is stored as plastic tensile-strain and is taken into account for reloading after an element has been unloaded (hysteresis). Due to the possibility of excessive tensile stiffness perpendicular to the first crack, the program has to store two plastic tensile- strains at each point (first crack and second crack).
 It could be that a crack has already emerged when a primary load case is taken over. In this case the fixed crack direction of the primary load case is used for the calculation of the stresses. For this calculation the strains in the direction of the crack and perpendicular to it are used. When a possible shear stress is present at the crack it is lowered by a simple friction consideration (Crack-toothing input with AQUA-CONC-MUEC).
 In case the primary load case was cracked and the tensile strain goes back to 0 again, ASE does not only goes back to the (0,0) stress point but takes into account a remaining strain of the crack zone. So a cracked girder remains a little bit curved after unloading. This is done by going back not to (0,0) but to a so called compression zero point. In ASE this point lies at 80% of eps-z (eps-z = strain reaching tensile strength). From there (0.8*eps-z,0) again compression can develop.

So a cracked girder remains a little bit curved after unloading. This is done by going back not to (0,0) but to a so called compression zero point. In ASE this point lies at 80% of eps-z (eps-z = strain reaching tensile strength). From there (0.8*eps-z,0) again compression can develop..
 The program takes the defined reinforcement as the default reinforcement. The non-linear analysis is then performed for the default reinforcement. An automatic increase in lacking structural safety does not take place! It is therefore the users responsibility to check the cer- tainty of the convergence of the analysis! Possible residual forces of the non-linear iteration have to be checked. Since these residual forces are stored as support forces they can be checked with the program WinGRAF, this is done by generating a plot of the support forces. During a plate analysis residual forces are also generated in the plate’s plane (normal forces), this is because the program needs to find equilibrium of the normal stresses.
 The reinforcement parameters and a given minimum reinforcement is taken from BEMESS- PARA or from the corresponding SSD design parameter dialog. REIQ is used to import a reinforcement from a previously generated BEMESS-analysis. The recommended method is used in the example a2_nonlinear_slab.dat . An analysis can also be made with non-reinforced concrete, when no reinforcement is defined. Further information on the program ASE can be found in the chapter ’Definition of Reinforcement’ as well as the latest TEDDY-Help .
 The consideration of the tension stiffening is done generally with a modification of the steel
 stress-strain curve described in [ 2] page 269. Since ASE 11.76-21 the consideration in ser- viceability limit state (NSTR SL/SLD) occurs according to the method of Schießl (DAfStB Heft 400) or EC 2, because more realistic deformation values result here. For the ultimate limit state and the non-linear determination of the internal forces and moments (NSTR UL/ULD or CAL/- CALD) the consideration of the tension stiffening is done according to the simplified method of the modified steel strains according to DAfStB Heft 525 / Heft 600. For a better clarity the in each case used method in ASE is output again at the non-linear properties of the plane elements.

For the ultimate limit state and the non-linear determination of the internal forces and moments (NSTR UL/ULD or CAL/- CALD) the consideration of the tension stiffening is done according to the simplified method of the modified steel strains according to DAfStB Heft 525 / Heft 600. For a better clarity the in each case used method in ASE is output again at the non-linear properties of the plane elements..
 Please note, that the serviceability analysis (NSTR KSV SL) should be done usually according to Heft 400 also for DIN 1045-1 and respectively acc. EN 1992-1-1, because it leads to a better agreement with the test result according our experiences.
 As the pure concrete layers also work in tension, the following working method is used:
 •
 In a first step the strains in the steel layers in reinforcement direction are determined. These strains are equal to the mean steel strains εsm according to Schiessel [13].
 • Using the tensile working law the two majoring strains I and II are determined based on the actual tensile strength amd the process zone length LZ (see below):
 I: average strain when cracking starts
 II: average strain for finished crack development = at the end of the decreasing part of the tensile work law
 • The streel stress is now calculated as follows:
 – In interval 0-I the steel stress is linear, concrete works linear.
 – In interval I-II the additional strain due to tension stiffening is interpolated linear. Con- crete descends linear.
 – After II the full effect of tension stiffening is applied, concrete stress is 0. Reaching the steel yielding point a trilinear part follows,e.g. the steel working law is used.
 • The process zone length LZ is calculated as follows:
 example EC=27700 GF_ASE=0.3 fctk=3.71: (EC=tangent at start of stress-strain curve)
 Process zone length LZ = GF_ASE*EC/FCTK/FCTK = 0.3*27.7/3.71/3.71 = 0.605 m
 In case you use GF in AQUA please notice that ASE internally uses a GF_ASE = 0.35*GF_AQUA. This correction is done to get better results compared to in situ defor- mations. In reality cracks that occur at the surface quicker develop to the inside of a slab due to stress range effects.

In case you use GF in AQUA please notice that ASE internally uses a GF_ASE = 0.35*GF_AQUA. This correction is done to get better results compared to in situ defor- mations. In reality cracks that occur at the surface quicker develop to the inside of a slab due to stress range effects..
 In SOFiSTiK this length is limited to 0.400 m, because otherwise an FCTK of e.g. 0.5 N/mm2 would result in a very long and unrealistic length. In ”Finite Elemente im Stahlbeton - Betonkalender 1993/I Stempniewski” a value between 200-600 mm is recommended.
 • With this process zone length LZ and GF_ASE a crack opening delta= 2 * GF_ASE / FCTK can be calculated. With eps=delta/LZ the length of the descending part will be DEPSX= 0.404 promille (relative to LZ). This value is then limited to 5*length of the increasing part = 5*0.134 - not controlling here. This strain DEPSX is used in ASE for the plot of the stress strain curve – that means for an element with the element gauss point size LZ.
 •
 In the real analysis now this strain DEPSX= 0.404 promille is scaled to the actual element gauss point size.
 e.g. element area = 0.05m*0.05m = 0.0025m2 = per gauss point 0.000625m2 -> element gauss point size L_Gauss = squareroot(0.000625m2) = 0.025m.
 – For an actual element with L_Gauss > LZ, DEPSX_GAUSS is calculated to DEPSX_GAUSS = DEPSX*LZ/L_Gauss (descending part is shortened).
 – For an actual element with L_Gauss < LZ, DEPSX_GAUSS = DEPSX. That means that the descending part will not be elongated!
 So for an element size of 0.05m*0.05m a descending part of DEPSX_GAUSS = DEPSX = 0.404 promille is taken into account.

– For an actual element with L_Gauss < LZ, DEPSX_GAUSS = DEPSX. That means that the descending part will not be elongated!. So for an element size of 0.05m*0.05m a descending part of DEPSX_GAUSS = DEPSX = 0.404 promille is taken into account..
 • For the new design codes (and without the input of CTRL CONC V5 400) the crack width is then calculated according to DIN 1045.1 11.2.4 or according to the Eurocode equation.
 The average force of the steel insert is calculated by multiplying the steel stress for the crack cross section in the cracked condition (state II) σs with the reinforced concrete area. This value is added to the concrete’s internal forces and moments.
 The crack widths are first calculated in the direction of the reinforcements using the eu- ropean coefficients according EN 1992-1-1 7.3.4(1) inclusive equation 7.14. If the crack direction is not perpendicular to the reinforcement, the crack distance and the crack width are modified according to EN 1992-I-I 7.3.4(4).
 For non-reinforced elements it is only possible to calculate the crack direction, but the crack width can not be established. To get an acceptable plot in WINGRAF, a fiktive reinforcement is assumed and with this a crack width is calculated. But this crack width is only qualitativ, not qantitative.
 For steel fibre concrete without additional reinforcement the crack distance es fixed to 140 mm. For steel fibre concrete with real reinforcement a correction factor 1-alfaf is taken into account (DAfStb-Richtlinie for steel fibre concrete, DIN EN 1992-1-1, new text (R.6)P and
 (R.7)P).
 The coefficient describing the connection properties is to be defined in AQUA-STEE. The factor for the influence of the load period is input in ASE-LC.
 For ultimate limit state the calculation is done according to Heft 525 / Heft 600, if DIN 1045-1, DIN FB 102 or EN 1992-1-1 is set.
 The shear stresses for the concrete law are not calculated for each layer, as is the case for the plastic yield criteria of STEEL, instead a simple shear limitation of the shear force is set with an assumed shear stress in the cracked condition (state II) of

For ultimate limit state the calculation is done according to Heft 525 / Heft 600, if DIN 1045-1, DIN FB 102 or EN 1992-1-1 is set.. The shear stresses for the concrete law are not calculated for each layer, as is the case for the plastic yield criteria of STEEL, instead a simple shear limitation of the shear force is set with an assumed shear stress in the cracked condition (state II) of.
 τ = q/z = q/(0.8 · h)
 (2.46)
 where h represents average of all the reinforcement layers.
 If the linear calculated shear stress τ rises over the shear resistance, the shear force is reduced accordingly and the element gets plastic shear deformations. By default the shear resistance is the bond stress FBD from AQUA. It can be changed with ASE-CTRL FRIC in N/mm2. Then with TAU2...V2 a descending part with a final strength can be defined.
 The shear limitation is only calculated for the centre of gravity. Then it is proportionally assigned to all the Gauss points.
 If a BEMESS calculation with punching occurs before the non-linear ASE calculation, then a check of the shear stresses in ASE is not done in the areas of the punching point. In fine meshes around a punching node also the support force is distributed to round up the bending (peak smoothing see following chapter and CTRL BETO V7).
 If this is not the case or if the permissible shear stress is exceeded at other singular points, an undesirable shear plasticity can be switched off with an increase of CTRL TAU2 onto e.g. 9.9 N/mm2 if required. Then a shear or punching check has to be done however separately.
 Procedure of a Reinforced Concrete Plate Analysis
 Usually the system is to be defined as a three-dimensional system, this is because the crack opening will cause horizontal node displacements, even in the plate analysis. For the special case of a reinforced-concrete plate analysis the system can also be entered as a girder grid SYST ROST - the program will then automatically introduce a horizontal statically determinate support.
 The first step would involve a linear analysis of the individual load cases, a superposition of the load cases and a reinforced concrete design calculation of the linear internal forces and moments. BEMESS will store the required reinforcement dimensions under the design case number 1 (see BEMESS-CTRL-LCR).

For the special case of a reinforced-concrete plate analysis the system can also be entered as a girder grid SYST ROST - the program will then automatically introduce a horizontal statically determinate support.. The first step would involve a linear analysis of the individual load cases, a superposition of the load cases and a reinforced concrete design calculation of the linear internal forces and moments. BEMESS will store the required reinforcement dimensions under the design case number 1 (see BEMESS-CTRL-LCR)..
 Subsequently a state load case has to be put together for the non-linear analysis. For the calculation of long-term deformations the load case components consist of self weight and a portion of the imposed load. A linear analysis of this load case is made, which is needed as a comparative reference later on. Now the non-linear analysis of this load case, under a different load case number and with a predefined reinforcement, is calculated (design parameter from
 The convergence of this non-linear analysis needs to be checked. The program finds a stable solution for the case where the energy remains the same (Energy convergence). Varying residual forces might occur due to inadequate convergence in the normal force directions. These are generally not of importance, but should be checked with WinGRAF...nodes...residual forces.
 The first load case of the non-linear analysis is usually calculated by excluding creep and shrinkage. Subsequently another non-linear calculation is made, including creep and shrink- age, under a different load case number. This is done so that the different effects can be compared and evaluated. It is also advisable to generate several calculations where the con- crete stiffness FCTK is altered, due to the fact that this parameter has a significant impact on the entire analysis.
 The entire analysis should then be verified with the following load case results:
 linear analysis of the state load case
 non-linear analysis without creep and shrinkage
 non-linear analysis with creep and shrinkage
 •
 Definition of the Reinforcement
 The input REIQ...LCR...FACT is used to take over the reinforcement from the design load case LCR, generated in BEMESS, with a factor FACT. But the amount of reinforcement is limited by a minimum and maximum value, defined in the design parameters in BEMESS-PARA or the SSD design parameter dialogue box.
 A minimum reinforcement is applied also without a REIQ input.
 The new reinforcement is saved under the design load case LCRS (default LCRS=99) and can or should be visualized and checked with WinGRAF.

Enhanced computation on singular support points in the material non-linear concrete analysis (SYST NMAT YES):
 Following problem exists: Such singular supports caused singular forces that could not be car- ried in the concrete non-linear material model, especially in combination with singular rotational constraints.
 At punching nodes from BEMESS now a first singular support or connection force (and bending moment) will be distributed on neighbouring nodes inside the column perimeter to simulate a constant distributed support pressure. Thus the feature only works after a BEMESS ultimate design with PUNC YES or PUNC CHEK! The support force of the centre is distributed via an internal coupling ring around the centre node and elastic springs to further nodes inside the column area.
 The processing is documented in the statistic print out "rounding singular punching nodes". It can be switched off with CTRL CONC V7 0. It only works on BEMESS punching nodes but also if they come from beam connections in a 3D analysis. It also converts singular connec- tion bending moments in a triangular connection pressure. The effect can be studied well by
 comparing a run with CTRL CONC V7 0 and a run with CTRL CONC V7 1.
 Especially at fine discretized punching points a rotational constraints will be analyzed more realistic (stronger). On such points the singular support moment caused a strong singular curvature in the fine mesh and thus a lower constraint.
 In a material linear analysis this feature is switched off by default, but can be enforced with CTRL CONC V7 1.

The image is a composite screenshot taken from the SOFiSTiK post-processing environment, showing how non-linear stresses in a quadrilateral “sandwich” shell element are visualized and interrogated. It consists of three main parts:

1. Main Mesh View (top of figure)  
   • A portion of an arched, concrete shell structure is displayed in perspective. The shell is meshed with quadrilateral (QUAD) finite elements, laid out in a regular grid.  
   • A continuous rainbow color map has been applied over the mesh to represent the scalar stress result (e.g. membrane stress σ). Cooler colors (green through yellow) appear in regions of lower stress, while warmer colors (orange through red) indicate higher stress magnitudes.  
   • You can see how the thickness variation and curvature influence stress distribution: the highest stresses concentrate near the mid-span of the arch, where the curvature and bending moments peak.  
   • The mesh lines remain visible beneath the color shading, allowing you to identify individual QUAD elements and their connectivity.

2. SOFiSTiK-Animation Dialog (lower-left inset)  
   • Titled “SOFiSTiK-Animation,” this small floating window provides controls for animating through different loading cases or stepping through the time history of a non-linear analysis.  
   • At the top are numeric input fields or sliders labeled “Magnitude,” “Speed Displ.,” and “Speed Rotation,” each set to 0 or “steady,” allowing the user to scale result values or adjust playback rates.  
   • Below these controls is a listbox labeled “Loadcase,” displaying several entries:  
     – LF 10 Bauzustand.5  
     – LF 301 Asym.Endzust.Linear  
     – LF 302 Asym.Endzust.THII  
     – LF 303 Asym.Endzust.THII.1.75  
     – LF 304 Asym.Endz.Zust.1.75  
   • The fifth entry (Loadcase 304) is highlighted, indicating that the stresses currently being visualized on the mesh come from that particular non-linear load step.  
   • At the bottom are buttons “LC-loop,” “Close” (to dismiss the dialog), and possibly a checkbox or toggle for looping continuously through selected loadcases.

3. SOFiSTiK Element Info Dialog (lower-right inset)  
   • This window, titled “SOFiSTiK Element Info,” reports detailed numerical data for the active element (QUAD-no. 2732) under the chosen loadcase (304).  
   • The upper portion lists scalar summary values:  
     – max.sigma⁺ =   1.6  (the maximum principal concrete stress at the “top” surface)  
     – min.sigma⁻ = –7.7  (the most negative principal stress, indicating compression or tension reversal)  
     – max steel stress = 86.5 (MPa, the highest stress in reinforcement layers)  
     – min steel stress = –25.4 (MPa, the lowest steel stress)  
   • To the right of these numbers is a mini-schematic of the QUAD element drawn as a small cube, with local x and y axes indicated. Colored thick lines on the cube’s faces visualize the principal stress directions at the top surface:  
     – A red line marks the positive principal stress direction;  
     – A blue line marks the negative principal stress direction.  
   • A “Node Info” button at the bottom likely allows drilling down further to obtain coordinates or detailed stress histories at individual nodes.

4. Caption  
   • Beneath the composite image is the caption “Figure 2.42: Visualization of the non-linear results,” tying these screenshots back into the user manual or technical report context.

Overall, the figure demonstrates how SOFiSTiK’s ANIMATOR module, together with element-level info dialogs, enables engineers to:  
   • Trace the evolution of stresses through multiple non-linear load steps (e.g. crack formation in concrete, yielding in steel),  
   • Inspect local failure indicators (crack widths, reinforcement strains),  
   • Extract exact numerical values for design checks, and  
   • Visually correlate mesh-based color plots with tabulated data and 3D stress-direction sketches for a single finite element in the model.

sections: 2.12 Non-linear Analysis of Plates and Shells

content:
The graphical output of the results over the thickness of the QUAD elements is another side effect of the consistent saving of the results in all the layers. The ANIMATOR can be used for the visualization of the results (choose a loadcase and double klick an element). The following picture shows the stresses in a single QUAD element. The element is a sandwich element, where the soft inner layer is covered by two harder top-layers.
 The next picture shows the non-linear stresses in a concrete arched shell. Here the cracks can be seen in the tensile zone. The thin lines are the stresses in the reinforcement layers. The significant numerical values, e.g. the maximum steel stress, are output in addition in the
 dialogue box.
 Example tunnel shell quads_on_fire_2.dat
 The visualization of the non-linear results from the steel and concrete law is still possible with WinGRAF, e.g. the visualization of the crack distribution at the underside of a plate, like in example of the reinforced concrete slab in cracked condition.
 The entire non-linear results, like the crack widths or stresses in the cracked condition (state II), can only be released numerically in the ASE calculation. For this the ECHO FORC record is used. For plastification number: see equation 2.45
 The available non-linear effects are logged at the end of a non-linear calculation in ASE in ’STATISTIC NONLINEAR EFFEKTS’ For plastification number: see equation 2.45

Usually a tolerance of 0.002 is sufficient for the concrete law (record SYST ...TOL). This tol- erance is also needed for the energy convergence. With negative TOL -1.50 a fixed absolute tolerance of 1.5 kN can be defined, if necessary not before 40% of the iterations: TOL4 -1.50
 The convergence problems in non-linear calculations, which consider the concrete law, could initially be solved by increasing the number of iterations (SYST...ITER). If after, for example, 50 iteration the energy still increases, the load can not be taken up anymore, this is because:
 – a lack of reinforcement (tensile forces can not be compensated anymore)
 – the plate is to thin (compression failure)
 – the elements next to the singularity are to small (shear problem)
 All these three problems lead to a point where the load can not be compensated anymore, due
 to an increase in strain. So the product of load·strain = energy will increase constantly.
 This can only be resolved by altering the system:
 – increase reinforcement
 – adjust the dimensions
 – decrease the load (try a lower load step)
 If the program does not reach a residual force equilibrium, even if the energy converges (the energy seems to remain close to the limiting value), then generally it could be attributed to the following reason: The program does not reach equilibrium in the normal direction of the plate - small changes in the strain plane generate large normal forces. Although this phenomena is usually insignificant for plate calculations and only has a local influence on the result. This becomes apparent when a check is performed on the residual forces (WinGRAF...nodes...residual forces).
 Often a damping of the iteration is successful with SYST...FMAX 0.90 (FMAX smaller than 1.0 or FMAX 1.10).
 If no convergence is found, the intermediate results of the iterations are saved with the load case numbers from 90001. They can be checked in the ANIMATOR with displacements and in WinGRAF with residual forces in order to find out the cause of the lacked convergence. With ECHO RESI 7 this can be enforced also for a convergent run.

If no convergence is found, the intermediate results of the iterations are saved with the load case numbers from 90001. They can be checked in the ANIMATOR with displacements and in WinGRAF with residual forces in order to find out the cause of the lacked convergence. With ECHO RESI 7 this can be enforced also for a convergent run..
 Often the convergence can be improved by the lowering of the concrete tension stiffness e.g. to 0.5 N/mm2. This is because the negative stiffness, on the decreasing curve of the concrete stress-strain curve, is not that big and it can be equilibrated by the positive stiffness of the reinforcement including the tension stiffening. On the other hand it is possible that a bigger concrete tension stiffness could instantaneously release a large amount of concrete failure en- ergy. This energy would then spread like a chain reaction through the system and convergence would be prevented. An increase in the minimum reinforcement would also improve the con- vergence, because the reinforcement would counteract the negative stiffness of the decreasing stress-strain curve.
 Steel plates or shells do not encounter instantaneous tension failure, as is the case for the concrete law. Besides being able to increase the number of iterations (SYST...ITER), one also has the possibility to generate a trilinear instead of a bilinear stress-strain curve, which has its advantages. The tangential stiffness in a bilinear curve is equal to zero, i.e. a strain correction of the program would not alter the stress. Another advantage is the slowly increasing curve, which is favourable for the Newton-Raphson-method.
 In addition the steel law allows a step-wise increase of the load, as described in chapter "bear- ing load iteration".
 For non-linear material calculations one always works with linear initial stiffness and compen- sation of the unabsorbed residual forces. An experimental material stiffness was implemented for improving the convergence of the iterations, but it did not achieve the desired effect and
 was thus deactivated.
 Non-linear material calculations, according to the first-order theory, utilize the Crisfield standard (CTRL ITER 0) in the iteration control. The line-search with the geometric-tangential stiffness matrix is only utilized in case of second-order theory are crack springs (CTRL ITER 3). The material matrix is always substituted with the linear initial stiffness and is not tangentially up- dated.

Non-linear material calculations, according to the first-order theory, utilize the Crisfield standard (CTRL ITER 0) in the iteration control. The line-search with the geometric-tangential stiffness matrix is only utilized in case of second-order theory are crack springs (CTRL ITER 3). The material matrix is always substituted with the linear initial stiffness and is not tangentially up- dated..
 You can always try both variants CTRL ITER 0 or CTRL ITER 3 but please start with the default (no input to CTRL ITER).
 In a lot of cases it is of interest to establish the maximum bearing load of a given system. To do this the bearing load iteration is applied. Here the load is increased step-wise until the point of failure is reached. The point of failure is interpreted as a lack in energy convergence, i.e. the system starts to fail if the energy is steadily increased during a bearing load itera- tion. A simple bearing load iteration can be found in example ase9_quad_euler_beam.dat , for cracked concrete also in the verification examples nonlinear_quad_concrete_beam.dat ( nonlinear_quad_concrete_beam.pdf)
 For non-linear material calculations it often happens that this automatic method does not reach adequate equilibrium, due to a lack in normal force convergence, even if the bearing load has not been reached yet. This can be overcome by entering a negative input for STEP under the record ULTI. Now the load is continuously increased, even if no convergence is reached after every individual load step. The user has to be assessed then the systems bearing capacity according to the energy convergence, the remaining residual forces and the load deflection curve. Alternatively the procedure could gain stability through the dynamic calculation.
See also YOUTUBE Video https://youtu.be/EvJuyYhPQKk and https://youtu.be/AJpfZ995lcs

metadata.sections: 2.13 Membrane Structures: Formfinding and Static Analysis

content:
Membrane structures are characterized by transferring of loads only with normal forces. Bend- ing moments and shear forces are not available. The analysis with real membrane elements is more comfortable and more exactly unlike the simplified processing with a truss model, be- cause the geometry and the stress state can be generated any exactly.
 Membranes should be generated with triangulas elements (SOFIPLUS export triangles).
 The first task is the formfinding during the analysis of membrane structures. A corresponding form is searched for a desired stress state in the membrane. A soap skin is only result here for the isotropic prestress. Forms which are different to the soap skin need a normal force distribution which modifies itself about the structure.
 For formfinding we do not use masses and no time step analysis, that means no transient anal- sis and no dynamic relaxation. You can better use the word ’force density’ but force density only works on the geometry alone. We (SOFiSTiK) use for formfinding the normal geometric nonlinear FE analysis with residual force iteration but with nearly zero stiffness in the mem- brane. That keeps the given stress in the membrane constant (soap film). As the stiffness is
 zero in membrane direction we use additional mesh control techniques to avoid a swimming of the nodes on the soap film.
 If the membrane form is found, real load cases can be calculated with this new form as initial system. The membrane must be omitted here for compression. Further textile properties are realized mostly by a simplified linear- elastic orthotropic material law. So when the membrane has its normal stiffness e.g. in a final wind analysis, SOFiSTiK makes a normal geometric nonlinear FE analysis (Newton Raphson and Crisfield or line search residual force iteration).
 Edge stiffenings with edge cables, inside cables or compression arches can be considered in real structures.

The image shows a three-dimensional finite‐element representation of a prestressed membrane surface, displayed in a softly shaded turquoise-to-light-green color map. At each corner the boundary is gently curved downward, producing a subtle saddle shape when viewed in perspective. The mesh overlay consists exclusively of three-noded triangular elements. These triangles are arranged in a quasi-graded pattern: element sizes are smallest near the centre of the membrane—where refinement is greatest—and gradually increase toward the edges and corners. No element interior angles exceed 180°, and each triangle remains well shaped, avoiding the distortion problems that can arise in quadrilateral meshes during formfinding.  

Because the nonconforming shape functions are switched off for membrane action in ASE, triangular elements here provide equivalent accuracy to four-noded quads but with guaranteed convexity. The surface exhibits smooth curvature transitions and carries the visual impression of an equilibrated prestress state—likely generated through an iterative “formfinding” procedure under isotropic or orthotropic tension. The corners arch upward slightly, and the centre of the membrane dips down, indicating a balance of membrane forces (NX, NY, NXY) transmitted across the surface.  

Subtle shading variations across the facets reinforce the three-dimensional geometry: facets oriented more toward the light source appear brighter, while those slightly rotated away appear in deeper green. The mesh topology is regular, with edge triangles following the curved boundary exactly; no gaps or overlaps exist. There are no beam or cable elements visible—the image focuses purely on the membrane shell, exported from SOFIPLUS as triangular elements.  

This visualization matches the recommendation for ASE membrane calculations: use triangles to prevent element inversion or concave angles during large strains and rotations. The triangular mesh also ensures stable numerical performance when large twists or prestress distributions (for example orthotropic or anisotropic prestress) are applied. In formfinding mode, the membrane’s plastic or compression failure settings (activated via AQUA NMAT MEMB or SOFiMSHA…QUAD…NRA=2) would govern whether compression loads are suppressed or allowed up to a user-defined factor.  

Overall, the figure illustrates a classic four-cornered membrane with a triangular finite-element discretization—an ideal configuration for capturing large‐deformation, non-linear membrane behavior in ASE while avoiding mesh pathologies inherent to quadrilateral elements.

sections: 2.13 Membrane Structures: Formfinding and Static Analysis

content:
The illustration is an oblique-perspective sketch of a single membrane finite-element that has been geometrically “twisted” in space and then overlaid by its isoparametric mesh lines.  Rather than lying flat, the element’s four corner nodes occupy non-planar positions, so that when the regular grid of parametric ξ–η lines (drawn here at equal increments of 0.2 or so in each direction) is mapped into physical space, the mesh distorts into a fan of nearly triangular strips that warp down toward one corner.  In the cropped view you see what looks like a triangular patch, but this is simply half of the full quadrilateral grid shown; one diagonal of the 4-noded element has been “pulled” out of the plane, producing a twisted shape.

At each of the outermost nodes (the two upper corners of the patch and the lowermost apex) a large arrow is drawn.  These arrows indicate the resultant nodal forces that the membrane stresses (Nₓ, Nᵧ, Nₓᵧ) generate when the element is twisted.  • At the lower vertex, the arrow points almost straight downward, showing a force normal to the deformed mid-surface at that corner.  • At the upper-right node, the arrow is inclined upward and to the right, following the local normal direction of the warped surface there.  • At the upper-left node, the arrow points roughly horizontally to the left (with a slight upward component), again normal to the local patch orientation.  

Taken together, these three force-vectors illustrate how a large, pre-stress membrane element—which by design carries only in-plane (membrane) stresses and no bending—can still produce out-of-plane nodal reactions when the element geometry is curved or twisted.  In an actual four-noded quadrilateral, a fourth arrow would appear at the “missing” corner, but here the focus is on the triangular half-patch to make the distortion and the directional nature of the nodal loads especially clear.  

Behind this sketch lies the mathematical fact that an isoparametric membrane element’s stiffness K = K₀ + Kσ (where Kσ comes from any initial pre-stress) will transform the in-plane forces into equivalent nodal loads that follow the warped geometry.  The figure succinctly visualizes that transfer: internal membrane forces are not confined to the element’s planar projection but emerge as spatially oriented nodal vectors wherever the surface is curved or twisted.

The image shows two side-by-side, three-dimensional renderings of a quadrilateral membrane panel, each discretized by a uniform grid of eight-by-six finite elements. Both panels share the same rectangular plan geometry and mesh topology, but differ in the level of prestress applied to their boundary cables. A thin, flexible membrane surface is shown in a light‐to‐dark blue shading that encodes either vertical displacement or in‐plane stress magnitude (exact legend not shown). In each panel, the long edges (front and back) of the membrane are tensioned by cables that impose an initial curved boundary; the side edges appear simply supported or free.

Left Subfigure (“small prestress”):  
• Mesh geometry: all elements remain nearly coplanar in plan, with only a gentle transverse curvature introduced by the boundary cable.  
• Shape: the surface bows slightly upward toward the midspan of the panel, creating a very shallow barrel‐vault profile.  
• Shading: a smooth gradient from darker blue at the edges (where displacement or in‐plane force is lowest) to lighter, almost cyan tones at the very center of the span (where the small bending or membrane action peaks).  
• Interpretation: indicates a membrane formfinding case in which a low cable force (low prestress factor P2 in the AQUA NMAT MEMB input) yields minimal out‐of‐plane deformation and largely in‐plane stress distribution.

Right Subfigure (“large prestress”):  
• Mesh geometry: the same quad mesh distorts into a more pronounced vault, with element faces clearly rotated out of the original plane.  
• Shape: the middle region rises significantly higher, forming a deeper, more pronounced curved surface. The front and back edges clamp into a tighter radius, consistent with a higher tension in the boundary cables.  
• Shading: central elements appear almost white-blue, signaling higher stress or displacement, while edge elements deepen to dark blue.  
• Interpretation: reflects a case where the boundary cable prestress (P2→1.0) is large, causing greater membrane strain stiffness (part of Kσ) and more dramatic formfinding deformation.

Common Details:  
• Viewpoint: oblique perspective from one corner, giving clear visibility of both plan and elevation profiles.  
• Element type: although triangular elements are often recommended for large-deformation membrane analyses, this particular example uses four-noded QUAD elements with NRA=2 (membrane formulation) and no bending stiffness.  
• Application context: illustrates how varying the prestress input (via AQUA NMAT MEMB P1/P2 or via HIGH reference points) controls the resulting form of a tensile membrane structure, a critical step in initial system definition for SOFiSTiK ASE formfinding.  
• Caption (partial): “Figure 2.45: A boundary cable left with small, right with large prestress.”

Overall, the figure graphically demonstrates the direct influence of boundary‐cable prestress levels on membrane curvature and stress distribution in nonlinear FE membrane analysis.

content:
The input image presents two side-by-side three-dimensional renderings of a simple membrane form (Figure 2.46 from the SOFiSTiK manual), illustrating how different levels of prestress affect the final shape. Both models share the same mesh topology—a roughly square membrane discretized into a fine grid of quadrilateral (and possibly triangular) finite elements—but differ in the magnitude of the initial prestress applied during formfinding.

General layout  
• Two 3D surfaces are shown on a white background, aligned horizontally.  
• Each membrane is anchored along its four straight edges lying in the horizontal plane; one corner of each “tent” is drawn upward.  
• A consistent color scheme runs from deep blue (at the raised corner) through intermediate cyan tones to pale sky-blue (at the mid-span and base edges), suggesting either displacement magnitude or membrane force intensity.  
• Fine mesh lines (wireframe) overlay the color surface, revealing the underlying finite-element discretization and showing how each element deforms.

Left image (too small prestress)  
• The apex elevation is modest: the highest point rises only slightly above the corner of the boundary.  
• The overall surface appears relatively flat, with gentle, broad slopes radiating from the raised corner.  
• Color transitions are gradual—deep blue confined to a small patch at the apex, quickly fading through cyan toward the lower edges.  
• Mesh lines remain nearly orthogonal and evenly spaced, indicating minor out-of-plane deformation and low curvature.  
• This illustrates that with insufficient prestress, the membrane barely lifts, producing a shallow, under-tensioned form prone to sagging.

Right image (too large prestress)  
• The apex is much more pronounced, with a sharp, conical peak rising significantly above the planar boundary.  
• Slopes are steeper; the surface curves abruptly from the apex into the adjacent elements, creating a more peaked tent shape.  
• Deep blue covers a larger region around the apex before transitioning to lighter hues farther out, reflecting higher local forces or displacements.  
• Mesh lines near the corner warp noticeably, with element edges bending inward toward the peak, indicating concentrated curvature and large rotations.  
• This captures the effect of over-prestressing: the membrane stiffens and tightens excessively, forming a sharp apex but risking element distortion or instability.

Context and interpretation  
• These two renderings serve as a visual guide for the user to select an appropriate prestress level in membrane formfinding: too little prestress yields a slack membrane; too much produces an overly sharp form.  
• The consistent mesh and color scale emphasize that only the prestress parameter—rather than mesh density or boundary geometry—has changed between the two cases.  
• By comparing them side by side, one can appreciate the sensitivity of shape and stress distribution to the prestress factor, underscoring the need for careful calibration in tensile-membrane analysis.

content:
The image shows a three-dimensional finite-element representation of a tensioned membrane under an orthotropic prestress state. The membrane surface is rendered as a slightly curved, nearly rectangular patch whose long edges bow upward and whose short edges gently flare downward. The overall shape resembles a shallow, doubly-curved shell with one axis of curvature more pronounced than the other.

Mesh and Element Layout  
- The surface is tessellated into a regular grid of quadrilateral (and possibly triangular) elements. Thin, dark lines delineate the element edges, forming a wireframe superimposed on the shaded surface.  
- Element corners lie on an approximately rectangular footprint when viewed in plan, but the arrangement has been distorted slightly by the imposed prestress so that grid lines are not perfectly orthogonal in three-dimensional space.  

Color and Stress Indication  
- A smooth blue color map is applied uniformly across the mesh. Lighter cyan-blue tones appear in regions of lower bending or bending-force components, while deeper azure hues mark areas of higher in-plane stress concentration or stiffer regions due to orthotropic material behavior.  
- Because the membrane carries only membrane forces (no bending stiffness), the shading primarily indicates variations in the initial stress‐induced stiffness rather than bending moments.  

Geometry and Boundary Effects  
- One long edge of the membrane arches upward, suggesting that boundary cables or high‐reference‐point prestress conditions at that edge have been set to a larger radius. The opposite long edge is flatter or even slightly downward‐curving, indicating lower prestress or a different cable radius in that direction.  
- The two short edges appear more gently curved, consistent with the caption “Orthotropic prestress – in longitudinal direction larger than in transverse direction.” Here, “longitudinal” refers to the long span of the panel, which exhibits higher tension (and thus stiffer response), while the “transverse” (short-span) direction carries a lower prestress level.  

Context within ASE Membrane Form­finding  
- This kind of visualization is typical of SOFiSTiK ASE’s membrane element formfinding, where user-defined prestress ratios in the warp (longitudinal) and fill (transverse) directions control the final geometry.  
- No bending stiffness (D-matrix) is active; only the membrane stiffness matrix K = K₀ + Kₛ (initial strain stiffness plus prestress stiffness) governs the equilibrium shape.  
- The smooth transition of element aspect ratios across the surface illustrates the nonconforming shape functions being switched off for membranes—triangles or quads behave equivalently.  

Overall, the render provides a clear demonstration of how differing prestress magnitudes along the two principal fabric directions produce a doubly-curved, stable form suitable for tension-only structures.

content:
The image is a three‐dimensional, perspective rendering of a rectangular membrane discretized with a regular quad mesh, used to illustrate an “orthotropic high reference point prestress” formfinding example. Key visual features are:  
1. Overall Geometry  
   • The membrane lies over a flat, rectangular plan view.  
   • Along its four edges the mesh is pinned (or tied) to an assumed support, so the outer boundary remains nearly horizontal.  

2. Mesh Topology  
   • The surface is subdivided into a uniform grid of four-noded elements, with visible element edges drawn in a slightly darker line.  
   • All quads are of similar size, creating a neat checkerboard pattern across the membrane.  

3. High Reference Point “Peaks”  
   • A number of isolated nodes in the interior have been assigned elevated prestress values, causing the membrane to bulge upward at those locations.  
   • These locations appear as conical or tent-pole–like peaks rising above the otherwise flat or gently curved field.  
   • In the example shown there are several such peaks (three toward the far side, one centrally in the mid-area), each forming a pronounced local maximum.  

4. Color Coding of Prestress Intensity  
   • A continuous blue-cyan color map indicates relative prestress magnitude or resulting out-of-plane displacement.  
   • The flattest regions along the edges appear in pale cyan, transitioning through mid‐tones to a deeper blue at the highest‐prestressed points.  
   • This gradient visually reinforces that the “high reference points” carry a larger orthotropic prestress than the surrounding membrane.  

5. Surface Shape and Curvature  
   • From the viewer’s vantage point, the front edge of the membrane remains almost planar and nearly horizontal.  
   • Moving backward, the mesh gradually slopes upward into the raised areas, then drops again between peaks.  
   • Where two nearby peaks interact, the membrane forms saddle‐like curvature, bending downward between adjacent high points.  

6. Interpretation in the Context of Formfinding  
   • The image exemplifies how assigning orthotropic prestress to selected high reference nodes will “hoist” those points into 3D space, with the surrounding elements adjusting their shape to equilibrate the stresses.  
   • Because the input prestress is orthotropic, each peak may rise differently in two principal directions, though here it is visualized with a simple symmetric uplift.  
   • The resulting geometry is stable under membrane‐only action (no bending stiffness), illustrating the kinematic freedom of membrane finite elements once prestress is applied.  

Overall, the graphic conveys a classic “cable‐net” or “tensegrity”–style formfound membrane, where localized prestress inputs translate directly into three‐dimensional deformation. It highlights the ability of the ASE membrane element to handle large strains and rotations, to enforce compression failure where desired (by suppressing compression in the prestress law), and to consider orthotropy in the prestress state.

content:
The provided sketch is a simple two‐dimensional free‐body diagram of a three‐cable connection at a single joint, overlaid with global coordinate axes, used to illustrate an inconsistent (i.e. non‐equilibrated) set of preset cable prestresses.  

General arrangement  
• Global axes: A rightward horizontal arrow labeled “X” marks the positive X‐direction; a downward‐pointing arrow labeled “Y” marks the positive Y‐direction. Both arrows originate in the upper‐left corner of the figure.  
• Joint symbol: At the center of the cable intersection lies a small circle (a ring) denoting the pinned connection or node where the three cables meet.  

Cable layout and forces  
1. Cable 1:  
   – Oriented purely horizontal to the left of the joint.  
   – Annotated “cable 1” (just to the left of the node) with a tension magnitude “200 kN” printed immediately beneath the label. The arrowheads or line thickness are not explicitly shown, but the label implies a tensile force of 200 kN acting along this left‐pointing branch.  

2. Cable 2:  
   – Oriented at some upward‐right diagonal angle from the joint (approximately 45° above the horizontal).  
   – Labeled “cable 2” just above the slanted line, with its tension “50 kN” printed directly below that label. This tension vector has both positive‐X and negative‐Y components in the global coordinate system.  

3. Cable 3:  
   – Oriented purely horizontal to the right of the joint.  
   – Marked “cable 3” (to the right of the node) with a tension value “70 kN” shown immediately beneath.  

Caption and interpretive note  
Beneath the drawing runs the caption “Figure 2.49: Illogical preset cable prestress can not be right.” This blunt statement underscores that the three annotated cable tensions do not sum to zero, i.e. their vector sum at the joint is nonzero, so no static equilibrium is possible.  

Connection to membrane‐formfinding context  
In the context of membrane form‐finding and prestress definition (as described in the accompanying text), this figure exemplifies how arbitrary or inconsistent inputs of cable prestress—especially at cable‐to‐membrane boundary connections—lead to unbalanced force conditions. Since a membrane element without prestress has zero out‐of‐plane stiffness, the system would be immediately unstable if the sum of all boundary‐cable forces at any joint does not satisfy ΣF = 0. The text warns users to compute and input boundary‐cable prestresses based on the target curvature radius via P = n·r, ensuring that the sum of cable forces closing at each node is in equilibrium before the form‐finding process begins. This example stands as a cautionary illustration that “illogical preset cable prestress” must be avoided to achieve a valid membrane form.

The membrane element implemented in ASE can be used only for calculations with large deformations with SYST ... PROB TH3. It is activated with the material input AQUA NMAT MEMB or with an input in SOFiMSHA...QUAD...NRA=2 (QUAD only with membrane action). The program configuration levels ASE1-3 are necessary for the material non-linear element and ASE4 for compression failure.
 Membranes should be generated with triangular elements (SOFIPLUS export triangles). The reason is that quads may get angles > 180 degree in the formfinding (problematic) and that cannot happen on triangles. And as the nonconforming shape functions are switched off for membranes, the triangles are as good as 4-noded quads.
 The membrane element described here is implemented in the FE program ASE of the SOFiSTiK AG. It has following properties:
 • The membrane element processes only membrane internal forces and moments (NX, NY, NXY).
 It bears arbitrary large strains and rotations.
 •
 It bears large twists and transmits the membrane forces from the twist into the right direction (here forces are available perpendicular to the thought element centre area).
 It is possible to use three-noded or four-noded elements for it.
 • A prestress can be defined (also orthotropic).
 • Stress modifications can be suppressed for the formfinding.
 It failures for compression (adjustable).
 • Orthotropic material properties can be considered (linear-elastic approximation). For anisotropic poisson’s ratio see example membrane_poisson_ratio.dat
 The stiffness of the membrane element consists of the normal strain stiffness in the element plane and of a initial stress stiffness from the prestress of the element.

 If the membrane should be calculated together with other structural members (walls, pylons, girders), the input is mostly urgently necessary with three-dimensional initial system.
 As in outline mentioned in chapter ”Overview”, the prestress is decisive for the formfinding. Different membrane forms can be generated with different prestressing states.
 This phenomenon becomes especially clear for boundary cables: If a boundary cable is more prestressed for a given membrane prestress, a larger cable radius will result and thus a smaller pass of the boundary cable:
 At high reference points a too large prestress ties up the ”neck”:

 In a soap skin an isotropic prestress is available in all points of the membrane. This prestress is determined about the surface tension of the liquid for the genuine soap skin.
 The strain stiffness disappears here in the mathematical model. The equilibrium results only from the three-dimensional equilibrium of the isotropic stresses. The stiffness of the membrane results to:

 The stiffness keeps the membrane in its form perpendicularly to the membrane area. Thought points are freely movable in the plane of the membrane area. For the genuine soap skin the phenomenon is visible at the blurring of the points (bubbles) on the skin surface.
 The in all directions constant prestress is input in ASE with the record GRP ... PREX,PREY (acts on all element types, also on cables, beams ...).
 Constant orthotropic prestress

For mixed systems the prestress is allocated therefore with NOG to the corresponding group. It is also possible to input some high reference points per group. The program generates then the average value from the inputs in each element in dependence on the distance to the different high reference points. In the following example there are four high points and one low point in a membrane area. The tangential part PTPR may not be too large for the high reference points, because the membrane constricts itself and tears off. The factor PTPR is input therefore different for the five high reference points in this example.
 If the distance is larger than 1000 m, the constant prestress is assumed with a stress in di- rection to the high reference point always of PR1 and a stress perpendicularly to it always of PTPR·PR1 and therefore without radial reduction. The advantage of this input is the simple definition of skewed prestress independently on the direction of the local element coordinate systems! The stress in the QUAD elements results from the global directions!
 Elastic skin
 A membrane can be defined from the beginning with the real stiffness and can be hoisted from the plane initial system at the high reference points or at the boundary cables. It results then large stresses in direction to the high reference points in dependence on the material proper- ties. They can be scaled, however, by using this state with the group factors FACL+FACS. The use of a elastic skin formfinding is described in chapter ”Unstable Membrane Forms”.
 Definition in different groups
 For membrane analyses the system has to be got already in the first step an information about a prestress in the elements, because otherwise the system is unstable - the stiffness is zero perpendicularly to the membrane without prestress! A load prestress is still not considered for the system stiffness. The prestress has to be input therefore with GRP or HIGH.

A load prestress is still not considered for the system stiffness. The prestress has to be input therefore with GRP or HIGH..
 The different elements of the structure like:
 • membrane areas
 boundary cables
 • structural cables
 pylones and other beams
 • massive support elements (concrete walls ...)
 are defined in different groups and can get thus different prestresses from GRP and HIGH.
 If different radii in boundary cables should be kept exactly (formfinding also for boundary ca- bles), then also the boundary cables should be defined in different groups. If the boundary radii were already input graphically (is absolutely recommended), it is possible to refrain the exact input of the boundary cable prestress, because the boundary cable force results from the radius and the membrane prestress during the formfinding.
 Criteria for the Input of the Prestress
 Free cable edges (free membrane edges reinforced with cables) should be input already as arch with the desired curvature radius in the initial system. The radius is preset in any case by the architect. If the boundary cable is defined as line in the initial system and the final edge circle should be determined by the program, then impermissible element angles are often available due to the distorsions. The iterations are much faster and clearer, if the edge arch has approximately the final position already in the initial system.
 The prestress which should be input for the boundary cable results to:
 cable force = membrane force radius P = n · r
 It is to be noted, that physical impermissible inputs do not arise. Unconsistent inputs can arise especially at the connection points of cables. In the following example an equilibrium is possible without an angle of the cable forces, because P1 > P2+P3+P4.

The figure shows a wire-frame view of a three-dimensional “angle” membrane initial system used for form-finding. Rendered entirely in red lines on a white background, two rectangular, planar mesh patches meet along a single fold line, creating a V-shaped configuration in space. Each patch is discretized by a uniform grid of quadrilateral elements (QUADs), whose edges and internal mesh lines are drawn as thin red strokes. The patch on the viewer’s left is tilted slightly backward and downward; its grid lines run roughly parallel to the fold line and perpendicular to an implied horizontal axis. The patch on the viewer’s right slopes more steeply, its orientation forming a sharp included angle with the left panel. Together they resemble two faces of an open book, hinged along their shared edge.

No cable edges or boundary cables are visible in the image—the only structural members shown are the membrane elements themselves. All boundary points of the mesh appear supported (no hanging or sagging cables), except for the lower free edge of each panel, which is left unconstrained to illustrate where the membrane could deform under prestress and loading. At the lower left corner of the view, a small L-shaped axis indicator (a corner marker) denotes the local coordinate orientation, hinting at the global X-Y plane and vertical Z-axis.

Because this is an initial system for non-linear form-finding, element stiffnesses would be set nearly to zero in the membrane groups (GRP 0 FACS = 1e-10), and isotropic prestress (SIGX = SIGY = 10 kN/m) prescribed. The program then iterates geometrically to find the equilibrium shape under that prestress. The illustration therefore represents only the undeformed, idealized reference geometry: a folded membrane of two planar portions, ready for form-finding algorithms to calculate curvature and sag under tension.

Visually, the mesh is free of distortions or element rotations, confirming that no boundary cables have altered element shapes at this stage. The fold line is crisp and straight, running from the front edge toward the back, dividing the two mesh panels. No external loads, dead weight or air pressure are applied in this snapshot—the image serves purely to define the initial geometry for subsequent non-linear iterations. The concise caption “Fig. 50: Three-dimensional initial system – angle” labels it as an example input (simple_angle.dat) in the ASE formfinding manual.

content:
The rendered image shows the result of a three‐dimensional formfinding run on a simple, folded membrane “angle” system, drawn as a red wire‐frame quadrilateral mesh. Viewed in perspective from the front-left, the membrane spans between two orthogonal support edges that meet at a right‐angle corner at the front bottom, with the other two edges rising and curving away toward the back. Key visual and geometric features include:

1. Mesh Geometry  
   • The entire surface is discretized into a regular grid of quadrilateral elements, drawn as thin red lines on a white background.  
   • Two families of parallel grid lines define the mesh: one set runs roughly from front corner to rear edge; the other runs from the left support edge to the right support edge.  
   • The front bottom corner is a singular boundary node where the two supported edges intersect; from there the mesh fans out in two directions.  

2. Overall Form  
   • The surface exhibits a characteristic saddle-like, doubly curved shape. In one principal direction it curves upward (away from the viewer), and in the perpendicular direction it curves downward (rising on the left and right boundaries relative to the center).  
   • Because all boundary nodes (except the free lower edge) are supported at fixed heights, the mesh takes on a smooth “folded plate” appearance, with a high‐point ridge along the back edge and a low valley at the front mid-span.  
   • There is no indication of cable elements or hanging cables; all boundary edges behave as rigid supports in three‐dimensional space.  

3. Visual Style  
   • The wireframe is drawn in a uniform bright red color, with no shading or surface filling, emphasizing the pure geometric form and mesh connectivity.  
   • Line thickness is consistent throughout, making it easy to follow individual element boundaries and observe mesh regularity.  
   • The background is plain white; there are no axes, annotations, grids or numerical labels in the image itself.  

4. Contextual Interpretation  
   • This output corresponds to the “simple_angle.dat” example for a three‐dimensional initial system specified as two intersecting planar partial areas (a folded structure).  
   • In the underlying input, all boundary points were prescribed in three‐dimensional space and the intervening mesh was left free to find its equilibrium shape under an isotropic membrane prestress (PREX = PREY = 10 kN/m) with element stiffness scaled to nearly zero (FACS = 1e–10).  
   • The formfinding run used quadrilateral membrane elements (AQUA NMAT 1 MEMB) and converged after a handful of nonlinear iterations, resulting in the smooth, doubly curved membrane shown.  

5. Usage Notes  
   • This wireframe is typically used to verify that no unwanted distortions or constraint-induced kinks occur during formfinding.  
   • Once satisfactory, the geometry can be “stored” as a new initial system for further loading, structural checks, or conversion to shell or cable‐supported models.  

Overall, the image succinctly visualizes the pure form-finding outcome of a prestressed, folded membrane in a simple corner configuration, using a clear red wireframe to highlight the deformation and mesh topology.

sections: 2.13 Membrane Structures: Formfinding and Static Analysis

content:
The image shows two side-by-side perspective renderings of the same folded membrane “angle” geometry, each under a different orthotropic prestress ratio. Both models begin from an identical three-dimensional initial system made by joining two planar partial meshes along a central fold. All boundary corner and edge nodes except the lower free edges are fully supported; the free edges are allowed to take on shape under membrane prestress alone.

Each surface is depicted as a blue wireframe of quadrilateral elements (QUADs), with grid lines revealing the finite-element mesh: roughly six panels along the “width” of each wing and eight panels along the “length,” for a total mesh of 6×8 on each side of the central fold. The quadrilateral mesh is uniform in the undeformed input but becomes smoothly curved under the applied prestress. The viewpoint is an oblique isometric angle, looking down onto the concave interior of each deformed wing and toward the central ridge where the two planes are connected.

• Left panel (caption “V-long/V-lat = 1 : 5”): Here the ratio of longitudinal to lateral prestress is low (1:5), meaning the membrane carries relatively higher prestress in the transverse (lateral) direction than along its length. As a result, the free lower edges bow downward sharply, producing a deeper “valley” curvature across the width of each wing. The central fold remains a crisp ridge, but the interior panels dip strongly toward the unsupported edge, giving a pronounced saddle-like cross-section.

• Right panel (caption “V-long/V-lat = 1 : 2”): With a prestress ratio of 1:2, the difference between longitudinal and lateral stresses is less extreme. The deformed shape still forms a concave surface but is noticeably shallower in the transverse direction. The free edges curve only moderately, and the overall form appears more uniform and less “cupped.” The transition from the ridge to the boundary is smoother, with reduced curvature gradients compared to the left model.

In both cases the mesh lines remain well behaved—no element inversion or severe distortion—even though the boundary is entirely free at the lower edges. The smooth, continuous deformation demonstrates the effect of orthotropic prestress on formfinding: by tuning the ratio V-long/V-lat (longitudinal vs. lateral prestress), one controls the amount and direction of curvature that the membrane adopts when prestressed. These two renderings illustrate how a simple folded angle geometry can assume dramatically different curved surfaces purely by adjusting anisotropic membrane forces during the initial formfinding step.

Left Subfigure (Plane Initial System)  
- Geometry: A flat, rectangular mesh of uniform QUAD elements arranged in a regular grid.  
- Boundary conditions: Four corner or support nodes are “hoisted” out of the plane during definition, while all other boundary nodes lie in one plane. No out‐of‐plane displacements are yet present except at those supports.  
- Prestress input: The membrane is assigned an isotropic prestress (PREX = PREY = 10 kN/m) and its eigenstiffness is effectively turned off (FACS = 1E-10) so that the only driving force for geometry change will be the imposed tension field.  
- Visual cues: Element edges are drawn in a slightly darker turquoise grid, the element faces are shaded in a smooth gradient from deep blue (lower regions) to light cyan (higher regions), but since the surface is still essentially planar, the color variation is very subtle.

Right Subfigure (Result of Formfinding)  
- Geometry: The once-flat mesh has developed a doubly-curved “soap‐skin” or hypar‐like form. Opposing edges have dropped slightly while the central area and the two other opposing edges have risen, creating a saddle‐shaped surface.  
- Boundary behavior: All original support points remain fixed in space; the free edges of the mesh have adopted curvature according to the tension field, producing smooth transitions at the boundaries without introducing rigid‐body motions.  
- Stress redistribution: Under the applied isotropic prestress, the algorithm has found an equilibrium where membrane forces balance out the geometric nonlinearities. The final element orientations are no longer coplanar; each element’s local coordinate system has rotated to align with the curved surface.  
- Color mapping: The height field is visualized by the same blue‐to‐cyan gradient. Darker hues at the four mid-side valleys contrast against lighter tones on the raised corners and the ridges, emphasizing the three‐dimensional relief.  
- Interpretation: This result demonstrates the “formfinding without further load” step. It confirms convergence of the nonlinear iterations (in the example it took nine iterations to satisfy the residual tolerance), and it produces a free‐form tensile surface ready for subsequent load checks or for use as the geometry for shell elements in a full structural analysis.

Overall, this two-panel illustration embodies the fundamental workflow of a tension‐only membrane formfinding: start with a plane mesh (left), prescribe prestress and boundary conditions, and allow the solver to iterate to a stable, fully three‐dimensional shape (right) that can carry real loads without unwanted in-plane constraint forces.

The initial structure can be defined with two options for the formfinding:
 • Definition of a three-dimensional initial system with at first plane partial areas: The bound- ary points of the structure are input three-dimensionally. The remaining areas are defined e.g. as folded structure. The program takes over the formfinding of the inner area.
 • Definition of a plane initial system: The structure is input two-dimensionally. At arbitrary points the structure is ”hoisted” then at support nodes.
 Three-dimensional initial system without cable edges
 Example angle, example file simple_angle.dat.
 A system is defined three-dimensionally from two planes (folded structure). All boundary points are supported, the lower edge is free.
 The membrane prestress is defined isotropic with GRP ... SIGX SIGY in kN/m during the formfinding step. Because the strains should not lead to stress modifications due to the formfinding, the element stiffness is set almost to 0: GRP FACS=1E-10. The QUAD elements with the material number 1 are defined as membrane elements ( AQUA NMAT 1 MEMB). ASE

 PROG ASE
 HEAD Formfinding for 3D Initial Systems SYST PROB TH3 ! for geomatrical non-linear iterations GRP 0 FACS 1E-10 PREX 10 PREY 10 ! prestress definition 10 kN/m LC 1 TITL Formfinding ! form-finding without further load END
 A load case with real 1.0-times stiffness should be follow after each formfinding load case for the check of the formfinding in order to guarantee that possible constraints do not lead to impermissible differences during formfinding. Furthermore an air loading from SOFILOAD must be updated, see example tennis.dat and air_volume_tennis.dat
