The image presents a three-dimensional, perspective view of a curved membrane or shell segment—most likely part of a tensile roof or canopy—rendered as a regular finite-element mesh and annotated to show local element coordinate systems. It is labeled “Figure 2.64: Updated system – coordinate systems.” The overall form is that of a gently bending, cylindrical‐arch-shaped strip, with its long axis running horizontally left to right across the screen and its curvature bowing downward (into the plane) or upward, depending on the chosen viewpoint.

Key visual elements:

1. Mesh Geometry  
   • The surface is discretized into a structured grid of quadrilateral elements.  
   • Mesh lines in one parametric direction are drawn in bright red, forming nearly horizontal “rings” around the curvature.  
   • Mesh lines in the orthogonal direction are drawn in blue, creating vertical or sloping “ribs” that follow the length of the arch.  
   • The outer boundary edges of the shell are highlighted in green, accentuating the free edges at each end of the arch.

2. Local Coordinate Arrows  
   • At the centroid of almost every element a set of small arrows has been plotted to show the local (element‐level) coordinate axes.  
   • The blue arrows correspond to the local z-axis (the unit normal vector), projected outward from the surface. These normals are roughly perpendicular to each mesh patch and vary orientation according to the shell curvature.  
   • In many spots one also sees very short red and green arrows (or thin line segments) at the same points; these represent the local x- and y-axes in the tangential plane of each element. Together, the triplet of colored arrows defines the orthonormal basis that would be used, for example, to resolve wind loads into local directions.

3. Surface Form and Shading  
   • Although the image is predominantly line-based (wireframe), there is a subtle shading or translucency effect on the grid that helps convey its three-dimensional curvature.  
   • No solid color is applied to faces; instead, the interlaced red/blue grid lines form the only surface indication.  
   • The background is white or very pale, ensuring maximum contrast with the colored mesh and arrows.

4. Contextual Interpretation  
   • This is the “updated system” after formfinding, meaning the structure has been pre-tensioned into its final shape and is now ready for subsequent load cases (wind or snow).  
   • The superimposed local coordinate systems are exactly the output produced by the ASE program command ECHO ELEM 4, which prints each element’s center-of-gravity coordinates and its local normal.  
   • The figure visually confirms that each element’s normal vector (blue arrow) truly follows the deformed geometry, which is essential for accurate spatial distribution of wind loads based on element orientation.

5. Overall Impression  
   • The combination of red, green and blue creates a clear, technical diagram—familiar to structural engineers working with membrane finite-element models.  
   • The regularity of the mesh, along with the consistent spacing of arrow markers, indicates a well-defined element layout, suitable for precise post-formfinding analysis.  
   • No additional annotations or numerical labels appear in the render itself; the caption alone ties the visual back to the program output commands and the underlying data file.

In sum, the illustration is a classic engineering‐software visualization showing a curved, pre-stressed membrane shell discretized into quadrilateral elements, each annotated with its own local coordinate axes and normal vector to guide the precise application of wind loading in further analysis steps.

The image is a side‐view wireframe of a tensioned membrane shell, labeled “Figure 2.65: Side view.” It shows a series of red grid–lines tracing the deformed midsurface of the membrane under a “wind pressure from below” load case. At the left end of the mesh, a short segment is highlighted in green—this represents the fixed support or edge restraint where the membrane is anchored and prestressed. From that support the membrane fans out and rises smoothly over its span to the right, forming a single–curvature shell.

Key features in the drawing:

1. Mesh Topology  
   - The surface is discretized into narrow, approximately rectangular shell elements.  
   - Grid lines run in two orthogonal directions: one set roughly parallel to the span (horizontal in the image) and the other approximately parallel to the transverse direction (shown bending upward).  
   - The element density is highest near the left (at the support), indicating finer discretization where curvature and stresses concentrate, and gradually coarsens toward the free edge on the right.

2. Deformed Shape  
   - Under uplift wind loading, the shell deflects upward. The curvature is gentle near the support and increases toward midspan, giving the profile a subtle camber.  
   - The red mesh lines trace this cambered shape, with the lowest point at the anchor (green) and the highest region near midspan or the free edge, depending on the loading pattern.

3. Support Representation  
   - The small green segment at the left base signals the support line. It likely corresponds to elements with full restraint in all translational directions during the formfinding and subsequent wind‐loading analysis.

4. Visualization Context  
   - No element normals or force vectors are drawn explicitly here, but the red mesh itself implicitly conveys local orientation of the shell mid–surface.  
   - This view omits any back‐face or underside details, focusing solely on the forward cambered geometry driven by the prestress pattern and uplift wind pressure.

5. Implications for Analysis  
   - In the accompanying text, this membrane is updated from a formfinding state, then subjected to wind from below (which, in reality, would tend to create folds if prestress in the transverse direction were insufficient).  
   - The wireframe highlights the geometric result of that loading sequence—an almost uniaxial stress field in the central region under full wind, with negligible biaxial stresses in some elements, as noted in the description.

Overall, the illustration succinctly communicates the final deformed midsurface of a prestressed membrane shell under non-uniform wind loading. The red wireframe grid makes clear both the curvature introduced by the formfinding process and the uplift deflection caused by wind from below, while the green segment marks the fixed support region anchoring the membrane.

sections: 2.13 Membrane Structures: Formfinding and Static Analysis

content:
The image presents two side-by-side renderings of a pre-tensioned membrane roof discretized into shell elements, illustrating how a uniform wind pressure from below translates into local membrane forces and element normals. Both views share the same color coding and mesh layout but differ in shape—one shows the deformed, wind-loaded geometry; the other the initial, undeformed form.

Overall Layout  
• The membrane is modeled as a regular rectangular mesh of shell elements. Thin red lines mark element edges in the local x–y plane.  
• At each end of the model two vertical boundary strips are highlighted in green, indicating support or edge constraints where the membrane is anchored to its substructure.  
• Blue arrows—or short vectors—plotted at the center of each element show the local normal directions (the local z-axis) and implicitly represent the direction of the applied wind pressure (from below).  

Left Subfigure (Wind-Loaded Shape)  
• The left image depicts the membrane after application of a pressure load from beneath. The mesh bulges upward in the middle, forming a shallow cylindrical‐like vault.  
• Red grid lines curve slightly between supports, revealing that formfinding under wind load has induced geometric nonlinearity: the original planar mesh becomes double-curved.  
• Blue arrows still point roughly outward from the deformed surface, but their tails remain attached to each element’s centroid, reflecting the local orientation of the element normal.  
• The deformation is smooth and continuous, with no element inversion or excessive distortion, indicating that compressive folds (if any) have been suppressed by switching off compressive stresses in the ASE analysis.

Right Subfigure (Initial, Pre-Tensioned Shape)  
• The right figure shows the initial, solely prestressed formfound shape before wind loading. It is comparatively flatter with straight grid lines in the center span.  
• At the edges, a slight curvature persists because of the transverse prestress distribution. However, the mid-span remains nearly planar, illustrating that only prestress (no external load) was active.  
• Blue arrows on the initial shape are all parallel and uniform in magnitude, signifying a homogenous prestress state and identical element normals prior to wind application.

Key Details and Context  
1. Element Center of Gravity & Normals: The blue vectors correspond to output from the ASE command “ECHO ELEM 4,” which lists each element’s centroid coordinates (XM, YM, ZM) and its normal components (nx, ny, nz). These normals enable conversion of global block loads into element-local pressures.  
2. Membrane Behavior under Wind from Below: Because the membrane carries only tensile stresses, wind-uplift pressures generate additional transverse tension. In reality, excessive uplift might cause slack or folds, but in the ASE model compressive stress branches were deactivated to maintain stability.  
3. Stress State Visualization: Although the arrows denote normals, the accompanying text notes that, for full wind, the stress at the center span is effectively uniaxial. Biaxial stresses are negligible or “omitted” in four central elements, meaning the local stress tensor has one dominant principal stress direction aligned with the wind pressure.  
4. Software Workflow: This figure is part of a larger workflow in which formfinding (load case 2) establishes the initial prestress geometry; then wind loads are applied via block or height-dependent functions. Finally, element-wise normals extracted by ASE support automated load definition, for example via table-driven formulas, in subsequent SOFiMSHA runs.

In sum, the image concisely demonstrates how a membrane’s finite‐element mesh deforms and reorients under wind uplift, how local normals are defined for each element, and how the initial and loaded states compare in terms of geometry and stress direction.

The image presents a three-dimensional finite-element visualization of a square membrane that has been “pulled” upward at its center, producing a pronounced bottleneck or neck-like protrusion. Key visual and structural features include:

1. Overall Geometry and Viewpoint  
   - The membrane is defined over a square boundary in the horizontal (x–y) plane, with its four edges remaining coplanar at essentially the same elevation (z ≃ 0).  
   - The camera angle is slightly elevated and oblique, looking down toward one corner of the square, so that two adjacent edges of the membrane form the foreground and background along the bottom-right and top-left of the image, respectively.  

2. Mesh Topology  
   - The surface is discretized into a regular, almost equiangular grid of quadrilateral (and some triangular) finite-elements.  
   - Toward the center, the mesh is refined into concentric rings of elements, each ring slightly smaller in plan area, guiding the viewer’s eye toward the neck.  
   - Element edges are rendered as fine black lines, creating a clear wireframe that reveals the deformation pattern and connectivity.  

3. Color and Shading  
   - A smooth gradient of turquoise-blue shading is applied across the surface: the outer, nearly flat regions appear in a pale, almost cyan hue, while the steeper, highly curved central region is tinted progressively darker.  
   - Subtle Gouraud shading indicates curvature: the inner slope transitions from medium blue to a more saturated, darker tone right at the neck’s rim.  

4. Central Neck (“Bottleneck”)  
   - At the geometric center, the membrane contracts sharply and then extends almost vertically upward in a narrow column. This slender column culminates in a small circular ring or hook-like detail (the point at which the model’s “load” or displacement is applied).  
   - The transition from the wider, gently sloping membrane to this thin neck is extremely abrupt—elements are highly distorted here, showing the classic “soap-film” pinch effect.  

5. Physical Interpretation  
   - The model represents a membrane or soap film with an imposed tangential prestress; as the central ring is lifted, the membrane forms a stable dome up to a critical point, beyond which a bottleneck develops.  
   - This shape mimics the behavior seen in formfinding studies where geometric nonlinearity and a small residual stiffness factor allow convergence even as the structure approaches instability.  

6. Context in Analysis  
   - This particular snapshot corresponds to “bottle_nec.dat” from the ASE program’s example set: a test to observe how increasing the tangential prestress (or lifting height) leads to divergence unless a residual stiffness (FACS 0.005) is included.  
   - Viewed in the Animator module, it visually confirms the onset of an unstable formfinding process: the membrane “neck” tightens and effectively pinches off, analogous to a soap film tearing itself from a small ring when lifted beyond a critical height.  

In sum, the image is a classic demonstration of nonlinear membrane behavior under prestress and displacement control, showing a square, fixed-boundary mesh that transitions from a gentle bowl shape to a sharply constricted neck, rendered in a turquoise wire-shaded aesthetic.

content:
The image shows a purely planar finite-element mesh for a two-bay “tent-roof” membrane system before any form-finding or prestress has been applied. Visually, it consists of two identical, contiguous octagonal rings (drawn in red) each surrounding a smaller inner support ring (drawn in green). These two annular regions are connected by a shared row of mesh panels so that the overall footprint resembles a figure-eight or two overlapping octagons. Key features are:

 1. Inner support rings (green)  
    • Each ring is rendered as a small nearly circular loop—actually a fine polygon—made up of contiguous green line segments.  
    • These represent the rigid or highly stiff boundary where the membrane would be attached to a lifting ring or support spring in the out-of-plane (z-direction) form-finding stage.  

 2. Radial mesh layout (red)  
    • From each green inner ring, a set of straight radial spokes extends outward, evenly spaced around the circumference, forming a starburst pattern.  
    • These radial lines define the element edges of quadrilateral (and near-triangular) finite elements modeling the membrane.  
    • The spacing between concentric layers of spokes is uniform; each ring of mesh elements steps the geometry outward toward the octagonal perimeter.  

 3. Outer boundary (red octagons)  
    • Each annular patch terminates in a regular octagon delineated by bold red edges.  
    • These outer edges define the free perimeter of the membrane—the “edge cables” or boundary supports in a tent structure.  

 4. Connection between bays  
    • Where the two octagonal patches meet, their outer mesh layers share nodes and element edges; this creates a continuous crease line or “valley” between the two membrane bays.  
    • That connecting strip is highlighted by the seamless red grid across the interface.  

 5. Mesh topology  
    • Although drawn in a flat, un-deformed plane, the mesh clearly shows refinement around the inner rings—more elements per radial angle to capture higher stress gradients expected there during lifting.  
    • Element shapes range from nearly rectangular in the mid-region, to more triangular near the inner ring, illustrating how the discretization conforms to circular and polygonal boundaries.  

Overall, this “initial system tent roof” layout is ready for the next step in the ASE form-finding process. In context of the accompanying text, this planar mesh will be subjected to an isotropic tangential prestress (soap-film analogy) and incremental lifting of the inner rings. As lifting increases, the mesh will buckle toward a three-dimensional roof profile—until a narrow “bottleneck” region develops so high in tension that convergence problems (ASE divergence) can occur unless residual stiffness is introduced. This figure (2.68) simply records the starting, undeformed geometry: two tent-roof bays with inner support rings and radial membrane discretization, generated in the plane.

content:
The image is laid out in two adjacent 3-D wireframe renderings, each showing a pair of circular rings linked by a continuous membrane mesh. Both renderings use two colors: bright green to highlight the rigid support rings, and vivid red for the deformable membrane surface and its mesh lines.

Left-hand rendering (undeformed or lightly hoisted state)  
• Geometry: Two identical circular support rings lie in the same horizontal plane, side by side, separated by a small gap. Each ring is discretized into an eight-sided polygon of straight segments (an octagon), with the vertices and supporting elements rendered in bright green.  
• Mesh topology: The membrane spanning from one ring to the next is discretized by a roughly rectangular network of quadrilateral facets. The mesh lines radiate outward from each ring, intersecting at nodes that form a flattened saddle-like surface between the rings. All membrane edges and mesh lines appear in red.  
• Surface shape: In this view, the membrane is almost flat between the rings, rising only slightly above the plane of the rings. There is no visible necking or pinch-in, and the curvature is very gentle. This corresponds to an initial lifting of 4 m, where prestress in the membrane and ring direction has not yet produced any localized constriction.

Right-hand rendering (4 m hoisted, beginning of neck formation)  
• Geometry: The same two green octagonal support rings now appear lifted relative to the surrounding plane, each ring forming the base of an axisymmetric “tower” or “neck.”  
• Deformation: From each ring a funnel-shaped membrane rises sharply upward. The membrane immediately adjacent to a ring is drawn into a narrow, cylindrical neck whose diameter is only slightly larger than the ring itself. Above that neck the surface flares outward into a shallow, dish-shaped cap.  
• Mesh detail: The red mesh lines faithfully follow the new shape, forming tight, radially converging panels around each neck and broader, more evenly spaced panels out on the flared caps. The constriction is most pronounced at the point of greatest curvature, just above each green ring.  
• Physical interpretation: This side-by-side comparison highlights the onset of an unstable “bottleneck” phenomenon in a prestressed membrane structure. As the inner rings are lifted, tangential prestress in the membrane cords causes a sudden local constriction around the ring, leading to a narrow neck and dome-like cap reminiscent of a soap film being pulled through a small hoop.

sections: 2.13 Membrane Structures: Formfinding and Static Analysis

content:
The provided illustration (Figure 2.70) consists of three side-by-side, red wireframe renderings of a membrane structure being lifted by a small, rigid ring (shown in green) to a height of 7 m. Each sub-figure represents a successive “further-iterated” form-finding result under identical loading and prestress conditions, highlighting the onset and progression of an unstable “bottleneck” phenomenon. Although the computed stress values are not physically trustworthy at this stage (a residual element stiffness factor FACS = 0.005 was imposed merely to force numerical convergence), the sequence vividly demonstrates how a soap-film–like membrane begins to constrict and nearly “pinch off” as the lifting height passes a critical threshold.

General layout and geometry  
- The membrane is initially laid out in plan as a broad, flat disc discretized into a regular mesh of quadrilateral elements.  
- Supports along the outer circumference hold the membrane in place; no additional discrete reference points are enforced in the interior.  
- A single, rigid circular ring (colored bright green) is attached at the membrane’s center by means of the membrane’s “neck” elements—these transmit the tangential prestress and vertical loads.  
- The entire assembly is visualized in an ANIMATOR–style wireframe (red lines on a white background) with the ring and neck oriented vertically.

Left sub-figure (“Iteration n”)  
- The membrane has pulled up around the ring to form a smooth “mushroom” or bell shape.  
- The outer span still flares gently downward toward the supports.  
- A distinct narrowing appears immediately beneath the green ring, forming the earliest sign of a stress-induced bottleneck.  

Center sub-figure (“Further iterate”)  
- With additional form-finding iterations at the same ring elevation, the neck under the ring thins still further.  
- The slope of the outer membrane increases slightly as load redistributes.  
- The wireframe grid distorts more strongly around the neck region, indicating large localized strains and stress amplification.  

Right sub-figure (“Final iterate”)  
- The membrane has partially collapsed: the neck is nearly pinched off, and the outer membrane has flattened back toward the support plane.  
- The ring remains at 7 m, but its load-carrying membrane has lost coherent curvature.  
- The combination of tangential prestress (PTPR = 0.50) and vertical lift has driven the structure beyond a stable equilibrium, visualizing a “soap‐skin” collapse.  

Contextual notes  
- In simpler examples (e.g. membhoch.dat with HIGH-0.3 prestress), ASE already diverges under strong tangential prestress; nonetheless an ANIMATOR picture can be saved.  
- In the tent-roof example (tent.dat), stable form-finding is possible up to about 4 m ring lift, but beyond 7 m one must artificialize element stiffness (FACS = 0.005) or risk nonconvergence.  
- The three images do not depict a correct membrane stress state, but they do reveal the visual signature of an unstable form-finding process: progressive necking and ultimate “clamping off” akin to a soap film drawn through a small ring.  
- This behavior is qualitatively similar to experiments where a soap skin suddenly detaches after critical stretching—here the computational model flags it by the dramatic inversion of curvature and the collapse of the neck.

content:
The image is a composite of six small “snapshots” (arranged in two rows of three) showing how an initially flat, elastic membrane mesh deforms as a rigid central ring is hoisted incrementally from 1 m up to 6 m. Each frame is rendered as a simple wire‐frame in two colors:  
• All membrane elements and their connections are drawn in thin red lines.  
• The central rigid lifting ring is drawn as a thick green circle (or short cylinder viewed from above), indicating the part that moves vertically.  

Across the sequence, you can clearly see the membrane’s evolving form:  
1. 1 m hoisted (upper left): the mesh has only a slight upward displacement at the center. Red grid lines slope gently inward toward the raised ring, forming a very shallow “hill.”  
2. 2 m hoisted (upper center): the central bulge grows, the slope of the mesh increases, and the red elements begin to fan more steeply. The outer boundary remains essentially flat.  
3. 3 m hoisted (upper right): the membrane’s sides become noticeably steeper. A low “neck” is beginning to form just above the ring, where the grid density in the vertical direction tightens.  
4. 4 m hoisted (lower left): the neck has become quite pronounced—there is a clear constriction above the ring as the membrane is pulled into a more conical shape. The wire‐frame shows red lines very nearly converging around the ring, indicating rising tangential stresses.  
5. 5 m hoisted (lower center): the conical peak grows sharper. The mesh above the ring is almost triangular in cross‐section, and the element distortion is more severe—some quadrilateral faces have become very narrow.  
6. 6 m hoisted (lower right): the membrane has tightened still further. The red mesh above the ring appears nearly collapsed into a cusp, and the “bottleneck” around the ring is extremely narrow, signaling that the prestress has driven the formfinding process toward an unstable configuration.  

All six views share the same oblique, isometric camera angle (slightly above and to one side), so one can directly compare how the curvature and element shapes evolve. There are no numeric axes or scales shown, and the background is pure white. Below the montage is the caption, “Figure 2.71: Elastic mesh 1 m till 6 m hoisted,” underscoring that this is a stepped animation of the formfinding process under increasing central lift.

The image, labeled “Figure 2.72: Cable mesh with the necessary structure clearance,” presents a three-view depiction of a conceptual cable-mesh footbridge designed for spanning the railway station plaza in Braunschweig. Rendered entirely in blue linework (cable elements) against a white background with minimal grey shading for ground elements, the drawing is divided into a top perspective view, a central plan (top-down) view, and a bottom side (elevation) view.

1. Top Perspective View  
   - Shows the double-curved geometry of the cable mesh in three dimensions.  
   - A grid of discrete cable elements forms a smooth, undulating surface that dips into multiple “deep points” and rises toward boundary “arches.”  
   - The four deep saddles (concave depressions) appear roughly aligned along the mesh’s longitudinal axis, with slightly raised “ridges” between them.  
   - Corner nodes at the mesh’s perimeter define high points; these are connected by taut boundary cables, creating an overall tent-like morphology.

2. Central Plan View  
   - Depicts the mesh laid out flat on the horizontal plane, revealing a regular rectangular mesh partition.  
   - Grid lines intersect at equidistant nodes, demonstrating the use of cables of equal unstressed length for simple assembly and measurement in the formfinding process.  
   - Small clusters of circular patterns around the deep points illustrate the locally increased cable length (added elasticity) needed to achieve sufficient sag and generate the double curvature.  
   - The outer boundary cables terminate at eight corner supports, shown as solid square markers, indicating points of fixed anchorage.

3. Bottom Side (Elevation) View  
   - Illustrates the mesh in its displaced form relative to the street level below.  
   - Grey rectangular blocks represent the required structural clearance for vehicular or pedestrian passage underneath.  
   - The mesh dips just above the clearance zone between support piers, then rises toward the boundary anchors, highlighting the compliance with minimum under-bridge envelope.  
   - The profile underscores how point-wise loading from the footbridge deck (not drawn) would induce additional localized subsidence of the mesh, a behavior deemed beneficial for static and dynamic stability.

Overall, the illustration communicates:  
• A formfinding methodology in which a planar, equal-length cable grid is transformed into a doubly curved structural surface by selectively adjusting cable elasticities—very elastic boundary cables to accommodate corner displacement, stiff interior cables to preserve mesh geometry, and partially elastic bundles around deep points to accentuate sag.  
• The concept’s ability to carry live loads with minimal additional deformation, enhanced vibrational performance through double curvature, and maintenance of a specified clearance envelope for traffic beneath.  
• A clear integration of analytical formfinding steps and practical construction considerations in the design of a lightweight, cable-supported footbridge system.

With the same methods formfindings can be done also for cable meshes. Discrete cable el- ements are defined here instead of the membrane. As for the membrane the cable elements can be used either as elements with constant prestress and known length or as elements with full strain stiffness and planned initial length. Latter one is mostly desired for the simpler fill- ing measuring of single cables with the same length. But it leads to distortions in the grid in the plane projection of the displaced mesh. The lower picture shows the concept design of a footbridge which is supported on a cable mesh - it is a research paper for the bridging of the railway station place in Braunschweig.
 At first the system is patitioned in an element grid in the plane with cables of the same length. The boundary arches are connected at first at an approximate form. In the following formfinding steps in which the corner points of the mesh are compulsory displaced into the desired vertical position the boundary cables were defined at first as very elastic. That means they might change their length arbitrarily, while the inner cables were defined with normal strain stiffness, because they should not change their position. The four cables which are generated around the inner deep points as well as single cables in the nearness are an exception. They have to be defined also partially elastically in order to get a sufficient lowering of the deep points and thus a double curvature of the cable mesh. These during formfinding more elastic inner cables have to be produced and installed therefore with a larger length. Foremost the double curvature of a membrane or of a mesh creates, however, the possibility to carry outer loads without larger deformations. The stability becomes thereby clearly better also for the dynamic vibration inclination.
 The point-wise loading due to the footbridge which is not shown here leads to a further local subsidence of the cable mesh. This is, however, favourably for the stability.

System input:
 • If possible, the system should be already defined three-dimensionally with boundary arches (set local coordinate system for the arches). The boundary cables can be used then with the full stiffness in the first formfinding step, because they have already the correct length. The three-dimensional input has the advantage that the span cables and the columns can be already defined in the three-dimensional system. Then the still inaccurate form should be smoothed by ”shrinkage” of the membrane - see -> Formfinding.
 • Without staying construction it is also possible to input the system in plane. Foremost then the system is hoisted by using the support displacements. In this way corrections of the height position are possible. The input of the boundary arches is indeed simpler. Because the cable length of a boundary arch becomes clearly longer during lifting, the first step has to be done with elastic cables (FACS 0.001).
